title: Five generations of computers — Computer Fundamentals
text: Five generations of computers Generation and core technology Famous machine and its generation 'First' in computing history Generation features and statements Ordering the generations Inventions and their years Computers are grouped into five generations . Each generation is named after the switching part at the heart of the machine. The order is vacuum tube, transistor, integrated circuit (IC), microprocessor, then artificial intelligence. Learn this ladder once and most questions answer themselves.

text: Memory hierarchy, RAM/ROM and cache Volatile vs non-volatile identification Hierarchy ordering and cache position SRAM vs DRAM ROM family: PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, firmware Cache and virtual memory concepts Fastest, costliest or largest memory A computer keeps data in several kinds of memory. Some memory forgets everything at power-off (volatile). The rest keeps its data.

title: Modals, imperatives, infinitives and questions — Active & Passive Voice
text: Modals, imperatives, infinitives and questions Modal + be + V3 Order becomes Let + object + be + V3 Negative order and warning Request: You are requested to Question conversions (By whom / Who was) Infinitive and gerund passives Advice and warning frames Modals (will, can, must, should) follow one row: modal + be + V3 . Orders use Let + object + be + V3 . Requests, advice and warnings use You are requested / advised / warned to . Questions start with By whom or move the question word to the front.

title: Let anchor
text: Let anchor An order (no subject, base verb) points to Let + object + be + V3. An option with no Let and no modal cannot be right. Active & Passive Voice

title: By whom first
text: By whom first Who-questions become By whom + was/were/is + new subject + V3 . Check the word order first, because options scramble it. Active & Passive Voice

title: Frame words
text: Frame words Please gives You are requested to . Advice gives You are advised to . A warning gives You are warned not to . Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Changing *Please help me* into *Let me be helped*.
title.right: Use the request frame: *You are requested to help me*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Writing *By whom this was written?*
title.right: Use question order: *By whom was this written?*

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Dropping *to* in the second passive of a two-object verb: *Homework was given the students*.
title.right: Write *Homework was given to the students*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Putting *being* or *been* after a modal: *must been obeyed*.
title.right: Write modal + be + V3: *must be obeyed*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Writing *Let the gate be open*.
title.right: After *be*, use V3: *Let the gate be opened*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title: Reverse conversions: passive to active — Active & Passive Voice
text: Reverse conversions: passive to active Tense recovery from the first helping verb Missing doer: supply they Object-case pronoun at the end Continuous passive returns to V-ing Let and requested frames go back To go back from passive to active, move the doer to the front and rebuild the tense. Read the first helping verb , not the participle, to find the tense. If no doer is given, use they . The old subject leaves in the object case.

title: First helping verb
text: First helping verb Read only the first helping verb. Was means past. Is means present. Has or had means perfect. Will means future. Is being and was being mean continuous. Active & Passive Voice

title: Doer hunt
text: Doer hunt The by-phrase gives the new subject. No by-phrase means they , people or someone . Active & Passive Voice

title: Object-case check
text: Object-case check The last pronoun must be in the object case: praised him , not praised he . Many options fail exactly here. Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Taking *was being chased* back to *chased*.
title.right: Keep it continuous: *were chasing*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Leaving the old subject in the subject slot: *The principal was praised him*.
title.right: Move it behind the verb in the object case.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Ending with a subject pronoun: *praised he*.
title.right: Use the object pronoun: *praised him*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Changing the tense on the way back: *was written* becomes *has written*.
title.right: Read the first helping verb. *Was* means simple past: *wrote*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Reversing the roles: *The window broke the cricketer*.
title.right: The by-phrase noun is the doer: *The cricketer broke the window*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title: Exam strategy: the 20-second conversion protocol — Active & Passive Voice
text: Exam strategy: the 20-second conversion protocol One clean option: fault elimination Tense trap among near-identical options Identify the voice of a sentence Combined skeletons Role-reversal decoy A voice question takes under 30 seconds. Use the same five steps every time: tag the voice, fix the tense, move the parts, re-agree the verb, and remove the options that break a rule. Each wrong option usually breaks exactly one rule.

title: Name the fault
text: Name the fault Every wrong option breaks one rule: V-form, being/been, tense, agreement or pronoun. Name the fault and the option is out. Active & Passive Voice

title: Five-row priority
text: Five-row priority Learn simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous and modals first. They cover most of the questions. Active & Passive Voice

title: Write it, do not just say it
text: Write it, do not just say it Voice errors hide on paper. Convert sentences in writing every day. The hand learns the pattern faster than the ear. Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Skipping the re-agreement check after conversion.
title.right: Always match is/are, was/were, has/have to the new subject.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Learning conversions word by word.
title.right: Learn them as tense rows.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Ignoring the pronoun at the end of the sentence.
title.right: Check the case of every pronoun. It is the fastest way to remove an option.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Accepting *is been* because it sounds like *is being*.
title.right: Continuous means *being*. Perfect means *been*.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title.wrong: Choosing the smoothest-sounding option.
title.right: Compare tense row first, then being/been, then agreement, then case.

text: [object Object] Active & Passive Voice

title: Cloze Test
text: Cloze Test · English Language · Verb form blank · Linking word blank · Preposition or phrasal verb blank · Word that fits the meaning · Fixed phrase (verb + noun) · Subject-verb agreement blank · Article blank (a / an / the) · Answer depends on the whole passage

title: What a cloze test is and how to attack it — Cloze Test
text: What a cloze test is and how to attack it Blank whose answer needs the passage's overall theme All four options grammatical: meaning decides The clue sits in a neighbouring sentence Option fits the sentence but clashes with the passage Verb blank fixed by a tense anchor A cloze test is one short passage with five numbered blanks. You choose the word that fits each blank. Every sentence in the passage gives clues, so a fixed method works better than a big vocabulary. Read the whole passage first, predict your own word, then match it with the options.

title: Tense anchor first
text: Tense anchor first Before you touch any blank, underline the time words: every morning, last month, by evening. Verb blanks obey these anchors. Cloze Test

title: Predict, then match
text: Predict, then match Cover the options with your hand. Read the sentence and think of your own word. Options are written around the right meaning, so a far-off option is usually wrong. Cloze Test

title: The read-aloud finish
text: The read-aloud finish After you answer all five, read the passage as if someone else wrote it. Grammar errors and logic breaks become easy to hear. Re-check any blank where you stumble. Cloze Test

title.wrong: Reading and solving one sentence at a time.
title.right: Read the whole passage first. Fix the theme and the tense before any blank.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Looking at the options before thinking of a word.
title.right: Predict your own word first. Then match it with the options.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Choosing an option that fits its own sentence but breaks the passage's tense or theme.
title.right: Check every choice against the whole passage.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Skipping the final read-through to save time.
title.right: Keep 30 seconds to read the finished passage. It catches planted traps.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Leaving the set half done and coming back later.
title.right: Finish the whole cloze set in one sitting while the passage is fresh.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title: Grammar inside the passage: tense, agreement, articles — Cloze Test
text: Grammar inside the passage: tense, agreement, articles Subject-verb agreement blank Tense / time-frame blank Verb form: gerund or infinitive after another word Article / determiner blank Adjective or adverb blank Pronoun blank Most cloze blanks are won by grammar before vocabulary. Three or four of the five blanks usually follow a grammar rule. The passage fixes the time, the subject and the structure, and the blank must obey them. Check tense first, then agreement, then the form of the word.

title: Strip-to-subject
text: Strip-to-subject Delete every phrase between the subject and the verb blank. Then apply agreement to the short skeleton. Cloze Test

title: Only-one-past trick
text: Only-one-past trick In a past story, one option may be the only past form among present and -ing forms. The anchor already decided it. Mark it and move on. Cloze Test

title: Say the article aloud
text: Say the article aloud For an a/an blank, pronounce the first sound of the next word. It is an hour but a university . Sound decides it, not the first letter. Cloze Test

title.wrong: Agreeing the verb with the nearest noun.
title.right: Find the true subject. Ignore the words between it and the verb.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Using a perfect tense such as *had joined* in a plain past story because *by evening* looks like an anchor.
title.right: Use the simple past unless the sentence truly looks back from a later point.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Choosing the base verb after a singular subject: *the city awaken*.
title.right: Add -s to the simple present verb after a singular subject.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Writing *an* before any word that starts with a vowel letter, such as *an one-rupee coin*.
title.right: Go by sound. *One* starts with a consonant sound, so use *a one-rupee coin*.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Using an adverb after *look* or *seem*.
title.right: Use an adjective after a linking verb: *looks attractive*.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title: Vocabulary blanks: meaning, register and collocation — Cloze Test
text: Vocabulary blanks: meaning, register and collocation Noun choice by context Verb choice by context Adjective choice by tone and contrast Collocation blank (verb + fixed noun) Tone check: praise or blame Near-synonym blank A vocabulary blank gives four options that are all grammatically correct. Only the meaning of the sentence can decide. Say the missing idea in plain words first. Then pick the option that names it, and check its tone and its fixed partners.

title: Name the missing idea
text: Name the missing idea Before you look at the options, say what the sentence lacks, for example: it needs the idea of consistency. Then choose the option that says it. Cloze Test

title: Fixed pairs to bank
text: Fixed pairs to bank Learn common pairs: gain momentum, pay attention, take measures, reach a decision, bear fruit, meet a deadline, break the news, strike a balance. Cloze verbs and nouns often come from such pairs. Cloze Test

title: Polarity check
text: Polarity check Mark the sentence + or - before you choose. A praising sentence rejects negative words, even when they are grammatically perfect. Cloze Test

title.wrong: Choosing a word that fits the topic of the passage but not the meaning of the sentence.
title.right: Match the idea missing in this sentence, not the general topic.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Ignoring fixed pairs and picking a near-synonym.
title.right: If the blank is half of a pair, take the usual partner: *pay attention*, not *give attention*.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Picking a big dictionary word when the passage is written in simple language.
title.right: Choose the neutral word that matches the passage's level.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Reading only the blank sentence.
title.right: The clue may sit in the next sentence. Read one line further.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Choosing a word with the wrong feeling.
title.right: Mark the sentence as praise or blame first. Then match the word.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title: Connector blanks: contrast, cause, result, addition — Cloze Test
text: Connector blanks: contrast, cause, result, addition Contrast connector (but, yet, although, whereas) Reason connector (because, since, as) Addition connector (moreover, furthermore, besides) Time connector (while, until, before, after, when) Result connector (so, therefore, hence) Pair connector (not only ... but also) Linking word after a full stop A connector blank is a logic question. The connector must name the exact link between the clause before it and the clause after it. Decide the direction first: opposite, cause, result, addition or time. Then choose the word.

title: Opposite-direction test
text: Opposite-direction test Give each clause a + or - sign. Same signs point to addition or result. Opposite signs point to contrast. Cloze Test

title: Partner hunt
text: Partner hunt Scan the sentence for the other half of a pair. If you see not only , the blank must be but also . No further thinking is needed. Cloze Test

title: Comma tell
text: Comma tell A pattern like clause, ___ clause with a one-word slot wants yet, but, so, for or and. Options like however and therefore fit the pattern clause. ___, clause instead. Cloze Test

title.wrong: Mixing up result (*so*) and cause (*because*).
title.right: Ask which clause explains which. The reason follows *because*. The outcome follows *so*.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Using *although* where a plain *but* is needed.
title.right: *Although* starts a subordinate clause. It cannot join two full clauses as *but* does.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Choosing a connector that fits the sentence but reverses the paragraph's argument.
title.right: Check the choice against the flow of the whole passage.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Marking *and* as always safe.
title.right: In a contrast context, *and* destroys the writer's point.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title: Preposition and phrasal-verb blanks — Cloze Test
text: Preposition and phrasal-verb blanks Preposition after a verb or adjective (fixed pair) Preposition of time or place Phrasal verb blank Preposition inside a fixed phrase Preposition before -ing (prevent from, insist on) Apply to or apply for Preposition blanks are about fixed pairs. The word before or after the blank decides the answer. Phrasal verbs are a verb plus a small word, and the small word changes the meaning. Find the governing word, recall its partner, and never translate from your own language.

title: Governor chant
text: Governor chant Underline the word that governs the blank and say its partner: depend on, afraid of, good at, solution to. About ten pairs cover most exam prepositions. Cloze Test

title: Particle direction sense
text: Particle direction sense Ask what the sentence does to the object. Does it cancel it (call off), reject it (turn down) or build it (set up)? The particle shows the direction of the action. Cloze Test

title: Substitute the simple verb
text: Substitute the simple verb Replace the phrasal verb with a one-word verb in your head. The sentence must keep its meaning. If it does not, that option is wrong. Cloze Test

title.wrong: Choosing a preposition by feel, or from your mother tongue.
title.right: Find the English governing word and recall its fixed partner.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Breaking a phrasal verb: *give way* without *to* when the sentence needs *give way to*.
title.right: Treat verb + particle as one unit and check what follows.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Mixing *between* and *among*.
title.right: Use *between* for two items. Use *among* for a group.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Writing *on* for a year or *in* for a date.
title.right: It is *in 2024* but *on 15 August 2024*.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title.wrong: Accepting a phrasal verb only because it contains a familiar verb.
title.right: State the needed meaning first. Then choose the particle.

text: [object Object] Cloze Test

title: Direct & Indirect Speech
text: Direct & Indirect Speech · English Language · Direct to indirect: statement · Direct to indirect: question · Direct to indirect: order, request, advice · Indirect to direct · Said or told? · Tense change and the exceptions · Pronouns and time words

title: Reporting verbs and the mechanics of the shift — Direct & Indirect Speech
text: Reporting verbs and the mechanics of the shift said to + listener becomes told + listener Tone decides the reporting verb Present reporting verb: no backshift One connector, the right one Suggestion with let us Direct speech quotes the speaker's exact words inside inverted commas. Indirect speech (also called reported speech) tells the same words in your own sentence. The quotes and the comma go, a joining word like that comes in, and the reporting verb often changes. So the first job is to pick the

title: Read the tone first
text: Read the tone first Before you touch tense or pronouns, name the tone of the quote: order, advice, request, question, joy or sorrow. The matching verb alone often removes two options. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: said to or told
text: said to or told Use said to + person, or told + person. Never mix them. Any option with said me or told to me is wrong. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Connector test
text: Connector test Statement: that. Yes/No question: if or whether. Wh-question: the wh-word alone. Order, request, advice: to + V1. Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Writing 'He said me' or 'told to me'.
title.right: Say 'said to me' or 'told me'. Tell takes its listener directly.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Using 'asked that' for a yes/no question.
title.right: Use 'asked if' or 'asked whether'.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Keeping the inverted commas or the comma after the reporting verb.
title.right: Remove them. Write the reported words as a plain clause.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Using 'ordered' for a polite request.
title.right: Match the tone: please = requested, advice = advised.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Backshifting the tense when the reporting verb is 'says'.
title.right: A present or future reporting verb means the tense stays the same.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Backshift: the tense conversion table — Direct & Indirect Speech
text: Backshift: the tense conversion table Present to past: the first step Past to past perfect: the second step Modal shifts (will, can, may, must) No backshift: general truth Frozen forms: would rather, used to When the reporting verb is in the past ( said, told, asked ), every verb inside the quote moves one step back in time. Am becomes was . Will becomes would . Wrote becomes had written . There are two exceptions: a general truth keeps its tense, and some forms never move.

title: Say the ladder aloud
text: Say the ladder aloud Present goes to past. Present continuous goes to past continuous. Perfect goes to past perfect. Past goes to past perfect. Will goes to would. Can goes to could. May goes to might. Must (duty) goes to had to. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Frozen five
text: Frozen five Could, would, should, might and ought to never change. If the quote has one of these, its tense is already right. Any shift is an error. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Truth test
text: Truth test Is the quote a law of nature, a habit or a proverb? Then do not backshift. Write: said that the earth revolves. Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Moving a past perfect verb up again (had had written).
title.right: Past perfect is the ceiling. It stays the same.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Backshifting a law of nature: 'the sun rose in the east'.
title.right: A general truth keeps its present tense.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Turning 'must' into 'musted'.
title.right: Must (duty) becomes 'had to'. A guess can stay 'must'.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Changing 'could' back to 'can' or forward to 'had could'.
title.right: Could, would, should, might and ought to stay as they are.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Shifting the verb but leaving 'tomorrow' or 'today' in the sentence.
title.right: Move the tense and the time word together.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Pronouns, and the time/place word table — Direct & Indirect Speech
text: Pronouns, and the time/place word table SONA pronoun mapping tomorrow / next becomes the next / the following yesterday / ago / last becomes the previous / before here / this / come becomes there / that / go Third person stays and gender check Pronouns change by who is speaking to whom. This is the SONA rule. S ubject-side words (first person) follow the reporter, O bject-side words (second person) follow the listener, and N o change for the third person. Words tied to the speaker's now and here also change. Tomorrow be

title: SONA sweep
text: SONA sweep Mark the three anchors before you change anything. First person goes to the reporter. Second person goes to the listener. Third person stays. Most wrong options break exactly one of these. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Yesterday and tomorrow pair
text: Yesterday and tomorrow pair Yesterday becomes the previous day. Tomorrow becomes the next day. If the option shifts the verb but keeps the old time word, it is wrong. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Check the reporting verb first
text: Check the reporting verb first If the reporting verb is 'says' (present), nothing shifts: not the tense, not the time words. Only the pronouns follow SONA. Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Leaving 'you' unchanged when the listener is named.
title.right: Second person becomes the listener: Ram becomes he.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Keeping 'yesterday' or 'tomorrow' inside reported speech.
title.right: Write the previous day and the next day.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Changing 'this' to 'the'.
title.right: This becomes that, and these becomes those.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Shifting tenses when the reporting verb is present.
title.right: With says or asks, tense and time words stay as spoken.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Changing a third-person pronoun.
title.right: He, she, it and they never change.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Questions, commands and exclamations — Direct & Indirect Speech
text: Questions, commands and exclamations Yes/No question becomes asked + if / whether Wh-question becomes asked + wh-word + statement order Command becomes told / ordered + person + to + V1 Request and advice frames Exclamation becomes exclaimed with joy / sorrow that Greetings, thanks and blessings Each sentence type has its own skeleton. A question becomes asked + if / wh-word + statement order . A command becomes told / ordered + person + to + verb . An exclamation becomes exclaimed with joy / sorrow that ... . Pick the skeleton first. Then fill it with the tense, pronoun and

title: Skeleton first
text: Skeleton first Name the type of the quote. Then write its skeleton: asked if ... / told ... to ... / exclaimed with joy that ... Pour the tense, pronoun and time-word changes into the skeleton. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Remove the helper do
text: Remove the helper do In a direct question, do / does / did is only a helper. It vanishes in indirect speech. 'Do you know' becomes 'if I knew', never 'if I did know'. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Exclamation map
text: Exclamation map Hurrah: exclaimed with joy. Alas: exclaimed with sorrow. Bravo: applauded. Good morning: wished. Thank you: thanked. Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Keeping question order in a reported question: 'asked where was I going'.
title.right: Use statement order: asked where I was going.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Using 'if' with a wh-question.
title.right: A wh-question uses its wh-word alone.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Writing 'He ordered that I go' for a command.
title.right: Use person + to + V1: He ordered me to go.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Using 'exclaimed with joy' for an Alas! sentence.
title.right: Match the emotion: Alas means sorrow.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Ending a reported question with a question mark.
title.right: A reported question ends with a full stop.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Exam strategy: the four-check protocol — Direct & Indirect Speech
text: Exam strategy: the four-check protocol Four-check elimination on a full question Reverse conversion: indirect to direct Polite questions with shall, could Word order and punctuation sweep Modal and time word together Every narration question changes the quote in four ways. Check them in this order: the connector, the reporting verb, the tense, then the pronouns and time words. In a well-set question, each wrong option fails exactly one check. Questions also come in reverse: you must turn indirect speech back int

title: Name the fault
text: Name the fault For each wrong option, name its fault: verb, tense, pronoun or time word. If you cannot name it, look again. If two options share no fault, you may have misread the tone verb. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Reverse-mode clues
text: Reverse-mode clues In indirect to direct, 'the previous day' means the quote had 'yesterday'. 'Asked if' means the quote was a yes/no question with the helper verb first. Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Write ten a day
text: Write ten a day Convert ten sentences a day by hand. Mix statements, questions and commands. In a week the four checks run together. Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Fixing the tense but leaving 'said me' in place.
title.right: Run the checks in order: connector, then reporting verb, then tense, then pronouns and time.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Writing 'had seen' unchanged in direct speech.
title.right: Step up one rung: had seen becomes saw.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Forgetting the comma and inverted commas in an indirect to direct answer.
title.right: Rebuild the frame: said to him, "..."

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Assuming every tense shifts.
title.right: General truths keep their tense. Missing this costs a mark.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title.wrong: Skipping the punctuation check.
title.right: Look at the last character. A reported question ends with a full stop.

text: [object Object] Direct & Indirect Speech

title: Error Spotting
text: Error Spotting · English Language · Subject-verb agreement error · Tense error · Gerund or infinitive error · Article error (a / an / the) · Wrong preposition · Pronoun and joining word error · Comparison error · Repeated or confused word · Question tag error

title: The master checklist: SVA → tense → article → preposition — Error Spotting
text: The master checklist: SVA → tense → article → preposition Divided sentence: find the faulty part Divided sentence with No error as an option Two suspects: the rule decides Fragments from different sentences Small word error in the last part An error-spotting question shows one sentence cut into four parts. One part has a grammar fault, and you pick that part. Do not hunt at random. Check the sentence in a fixed order, because most errors sit in the first four checks.

title: The sweep in one line
text: The sweep in one line Verb first: find the subject and check its number. Then tense words. Then a / an / the by sound. Then the preposition partner. Only then pronouns, pairs and word choice. Error Spotting

title: Strip the middle
text: Strip the middle Delete the phrase between the subject and the verb, such as 'of my friends' or 'as well as the players'. Read the bare skeleton. Agreement errors become loud. Error Spotting

title: Earn the No error answer
text: Earn the No error answer Choose 'No error' only after the full sweep. About one in five of these items hides a quiet agreement or preposition fault. Error Spotting

title.wrong: Matching the verb with the noun nearest to it.
title.right: Find the true subject. Cover the phrase in between.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Marking the part that only sounds clumsy.
title.right: Awkward is not always wrong. Mark only a part that breaks a named rule.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Starting the hunt in the middle and skipping the first part.
title.right: Check the first part too. Pronoun and connector errors sit there.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Finding two errors and freezing.
title.right: Re-check the second one. It is usually standard usage you misjudged.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Choosing 'No error' because the sentence sounds fine at speed.
title.right: Run all eight checks before you choose it.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Subject–verb agreement errors — Error Spotting
text: Subject–verb agreement errors One of / every one of + plural noun Either ... or / neither ... nor Each / every / many a + singular verb A number of and the number of Verb after who / which / that Special singular subjects Agreement errors are the biggest error family in SSC English. The verb must match the true subject in number. The trap is always the same: extra words sit between the subject and the verb. Cover those words and match the verb with what is left.

title: Hunt the subject backwards
text: Hunt the subject backwards Start at the verb and walk backwards past every 'of ...' phrase. The first noun or pronoun with no preposition in front is the subject. Error Spotting

title: Nearness rule flash
text: Nearness rule flash See neither ... nor or either ... or with two subjects? The verb matches the second one. The item usually solves at once. Error Spotting

title: A quantity is singular
text: A quantity is singular Money, distance, time and weight taken as one amount use a singular verb, even in plural form: 'Ten kilometres is a long walk.' Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using a plural verb after each, every or either ('Each of the boys have').
title.right: Each, every and either are singular. Say 'Each of the boys has'.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Treating 'a number of' and 'the number of' as the same.
title.right: A number of = plural verb. The number of = singular verb.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Making news, mathematics and physics plural because they end in -s.
title.right: They are singular. The news is good.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'one of my friends who works' when the who-clause needs the plural.
title.right: In 'one of those officers who work', the pronoun points to 'officers'.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Agreeing the verb with the noun after 'as well as' or 'along with'.
title.right: The verb follows the first subject.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Tense and sequence-of-tenses errors — Error Spotting
text: Tense and sequence-of-tenses errors Will inside a when / if / until clause Since vs for Past perfect for the earlier past event Present perfect with a finished time General truth pulled into the past Past reporting verb, unchanged verb inside Every sentence has a time word (an anchor ) such as yesterday, since 2019 or when. The verb must obey it. Tense errors have a few fixed shapes. Look for will inside a time clause. Look for since and for mixed up. Look for a missing past perfect, and for a perfect tense next to a finished time.

title: Circle every anchor
text: Circle every anchor Circle yesterday, ago, since, for, by the time, when and next week before you judge any verb. Most tense items solve themselves. Error Spotting

title: The will check
text: The will check Scan for will inside a when / if / until clause with future meaning. SSC plants this error again and again. Error Spotting

title: Since and for sorting
text: Since and for sorting Since + starting point (since Monday, since 2019, since childhood). For + length (for ten years, for a week). The wrong partner is the answer. Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using the present perfect with a finished time ('I have met him yesterday').
title.right: Use the simple past: 'I met him yesterday'.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Moving only half the sentence back: 'He said he will come'.
title.right: Move the whole clause back: 'He said he would come'.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using the past perfect whenever two past verbs appear.
title.right: Use it only to show which action came first.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'since' with a length of time because it sounds formal.
title.right: Length takes 'for': for ten years.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Putting will inside the when-clause.
title.right: Use the simple present in the when-clause. Keep will in the main clause.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Article and preposition errors — Error Spotting
text: Article and preposition errors A vs an by sound The with superlatives and unique nouns Adjective + fixed preposition Verb + fixed preposition Time, place and between / among Extra article before a language, meal or game Articles are a sound decision. Use a or an by the first sound of the next word, not its first letter. Use the for a known, unique or superlative noun. Prepositions are fixed partners: find the word the preposition depends on, and recall its usual partner.

title: Say it aloud
text: Say it aloud Articles are sound decisions. Say the phrase. 'An university' fails the ear because of the 'yu' sound. 'A honest man' fails too. Error Spotting

title: Governor chant
text: Governor chant Underline the word the preposition depends on. Recite its partner: insist on, angry with (person), prefer to, married to. A wrong partner is the answer. Error Spotting

title: The with superlatives
text: The with superlatives Superlatives and ordinals need the: 'the most intelligent girl', 'the first attempt'. A bare superlative hides an article error. Error Spotting

title.wrong: Choosing 'an' for words that start with a vowel letter but a consonant sound (university, union, one).
title.right: Go by sound: a university, a union, a one-rupee coin.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using 'than' after senior, junior, superior, inferior or prefer.
title.right: These words take 'to'.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'angry on him' or 'consists in students' by literal translation.
title.right: Learn the fixed pair: angry with him, consists of students.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Adding 'the' before school, hospital or home in the purpose sense.
title.right: Say 'go to school' when you mean attend.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using 'a best' or 'a most'.
title.right: A superlative takes 'the'.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Pronoun and correlative-conjunction errors — Error Spotting
text: Pronoun and correlative-conjunction errors Pronoun case after a preposition or let Who / whom / whose / which Correlative pair mismatch Its / it's and other look-alikes Connective in reported questions Myself as a subject; a repeated pronoun Pronouns change form by their job: subject forms do the action, object forms receive it. Correlative pairs such as no sooner ... than always travel together. Most errors are the wrong pronoun case, the wrong partner word, or a wrong connective in reported speech.

title: Preposition plus I? Kill it
text: Preposition plus I? Kill it Between you and I, for he and I: all wrong. After a preposition, use the object form every time. Error Spotting

title: Did plus base form
text: Did plus base form After did, does or do, the verb keeps its base form: 'No sooner did the bell ring'. A past form after did is always an error. Error Spotting

title: Cover and match the pair
text: Cover and match the pair Cover everything except the pair words. If one half stands with the wrong partner (hardly ... than), that part is the error. Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using 'whom' as the subject, or 'who' after a preposition ('to who').
title.right: Subject: who. After a preposition or as object: whom.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'between him and she'.
title.right: Both pronouns after 'between' are objects: between him and her.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Pairing hardly / scarcely with 'than' and no sooner with 'when'.
title.right: Hardly / scarcely go with when. No sooner goes with than.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Marking 'everyone ... their' without knowing the key.
title.right: SSC keys follow his / her. Mark accordingly when the options force a choice.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'that whether' or 'that why' in a reported question.
title.right: Use 'whether' or 'why' alone.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Comparison, redundancy and confusable-word errors — Error Spotting
text: Comparison, redundancy and confusable-word errors Double or mixed comparative forms Redundant word pairs Confusable word swap Comparison logic: any other, that of, to Few, little, fewer, less and elder Verbs that need no preposition Comparison errors are double forms ( more bigger ), broken logic ( bigger than any city ) and a wrong than after Latin words like superior . Word-choice errors are repeated ideas ( return back ) and look-alike words ( advice, advise ). Learn the short lists below and the errors show up at once.

title: Scan for more + er
text: Scan for more + er Look for more before a comparative (more bigger) or most before a superlative. That is an error at once. Error Spotting

title: Flinch at echo pairs
text: Flinch at echo pairs In pairs like return back, repeat again and revert back, the second word repeats the first. These are planted answers. Error Spotting

title: The that-of test
text: The that-of test When two nouns' qualities are compared, the second noun needs that of or those of: 'The roads of Delhi are wider than those of Patna.' Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'Mumbai is bigger than any city in India'.
title.right: Add 'other': bigger than any other city in India.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Using 'than' after prefer, senior, junior, superior or inferior.
title.right: These take 'to' only.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Treating 'a little' and 'a few' as errors.
title.right: They are positive forms. Only 'little' and 'few' alone are negative.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Marking a long phrase as redundant just because it is wordy.
title.right: SSC items mark echo pairs like return back, not every long phrase.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Comparing a quality with a place ('cooler than Bengaluru').
title.right: Use that of / those of: cooler than that of Bengaluru.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Verb forms, question tags, conditionals and structure — Error Spotting
text: Verb forms, question tags, conditionals and structure Gerund or infinitive after a verb or preposition Question tag sign and pronoun Conditional half broken Broken parallelism in a list Adjective or adverb after a verb Modal + to or able to These errors are not about agreement, tense, articles or prepositions. They sit in the shape of the sentence. Check the verb after another verb (-ing or to), the tag at the end, the two halves of an if-sentence, the shape of a list, adjective versus adverb, and modals.

title: Flip the tag
text: Flip the tag Hear the end of the sentence. A positive statement needs a negative tag. A negative word (never, rarely, hardly) needs a positive tag. Error Spotting

title: Unreal past conditional
text: Unreal past conditional After 'if' about the unreal past, use had + participle. 'Would have' in the if-part is the planted error. Error Spotting

title: Copy the first item
text: Copy the first item In a list, the first item sets the shape (-ing, to + verb or noun). Every other item must copy it. Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'could able to' or 'can able to'.
title.right: Can and could already carry ability. Use the base verb only.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'He denied to take the file'.
title.right: Deny, enjoy, avoid and suggest take -ing: denied taking.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Tagging a positive statement with a positive tag ('They have come, isn't it?').
title.right: Flip the sign and match the pronoun: haven't they?

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Putting would have inside the if-part of an unreal past.
title.right: Use had + participle in the if-part.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title.wrong: Writing 'look forward to meet'.
title.right: Here 'to' is a preposition. Say look forward to meeting.

text: [object Object] Error Spotting

title: Fill in the Blanks
text: Fill in the Blanks · English Language · Verb + noun phrase · Adjective + noun phrase · Look-alike words · Phrasal verb blank · Verb form and tense · Joining word or relative pronoun · Two blanks together · Hardly / No sooner

title: Collocation blanks: word partnerships that decide the answer — Fill in the Blanks
text: Collocation blanks: word partnerships that decide the answer do / make / take / give / pay swap Adjective + noun pair Illness and feeling reactions Fixed expressions (break the news, a narrow escape) reach / meet / strike + result nouns Word + fixed preposition Formal adjective + noun (abject poverty) A collocation is a pair of words that English always uses together, like pay attention or heavy rain . In these blanks, most options fit the grammar. Only one option is the usual partner of the word next to the blank. So you pick the partner, not just a word with the right meaning.

title: Answer before you look at the options
text: Answer before you look at the options Read up to the blank and stop. Ask what the word before it usually takes. Say your answer, then find it among the options. Fill in the Blanks

title: Cut options by topic
text: Cut options by topic Collocation options often share an ending (-tion, -ment). Remove the ones that do not suit the topic first. A border dispute invites talks or deliberations, never medications. Fill in the Blanks

title: Finish the phrase in your head
text: Finish the phrase in your head For a verb blank, turn the phrase around: 'attention is ___' gives 'paid'. If your word is an option, mark it and move on. Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Choosing a synonym that breaks the pair, such as 'give attention'.
title.right: Pick the fixed partner: pay attention, take place, commit a crime.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Choosing the longest or most impressive word.
title.right: The collocation answer is usually an ordinary, everyday word.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Ignoring the preposition after the blank ('___ on', '___ with').
title.right: Let the preposition fix the chunk: emphasis on, comply with, abide by.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Treating near-synonym adjectives as equal (strong rain, quick asleep).
title.right: Learn the adjective with its noun: heavy rain, fast asleep, narrow escape.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Answering after reading only half the sentence.
title.right: Read to the full stop. A later phrase often decides between two real pairs.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title: Phrasal-verb blanks: verb + particle as one unit — Fill in the Blanks
text: Phrasal-verb blanks: verb + particle as one unit Same verb, different small words look-family blanks put-family blanks Mixed common phrasal verbs look forward to / be used to / object to + -ing break and run families A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word like off , up or into . Together they make a new meaning. Call off means cancel; it has nothing to do with calling. So first find the meaning the sentence needs, then pick the verb and small word that carry it.

title: Say the meaning in one word, then match
text: Say the meaning in one word, then match Put the sentence's action in one plain word: cancelled, tolerated, abolished. Then pick the phrasal verb that means that word. Fill in the Blanks

title: Swap in a one-word verb
text: Swap in a one-word verb Replace each option with a one-word verb (call off = cancel, turn down = reject). The option whose swap keeps the meaning is right. Fill in the Blanks

title: Use the direction of the small word
text: Use the direction of the small word Ask what happens to the object: stopped or removed (off, out), raised (up), lowered or refused (down), accepted (in). Match that to the particle. Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Picking the particle your first language would use.
title.right: Learn each phrasal verb as one unit with its English meaning.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Mixing 'put up with' (tolerate) and 'put off' (postpone) because both start with 'put'.
title.right: Say the meaning first, then choose: tolerate = put up with, postpone = put off.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Reading only the clause with the blank.
title.right: Read the whole sentence; the doer and the reason are often in the other clause.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Writing 'was broken out' for a fire or a war.
title.right: Break out has no passive: 'a fire broke out'.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Writing 'look forward to meet you'.
title.right: The 'to' here is a preposition: look forward to meeting you.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title: Verb-form and tense blanks — Fill in the Blanks
text: Verb-form and tense blanks since / for with perfect tenses Past perfect + simple past If-sentences -ing or to + verb after a fixed verb Agreement blanks (each of, the number of) used to / be used to / had better by + future time When the blank is a verb, two things decide the answer. First, the time words in the sentence (since, yesterday, by the time) pick the tense. Second, the word just before the blank can fix the form: -ing, to + verb, or the plain verb.

title: Who owns the 'to'?
text: Who owns the 'to'? If 'to' belongs to a phrase like look forward to or object to, it is a preposition, so use -ing. If it belongs to a verb like decide or hope, use the base verb. Fill in the Blanks

title: The by-the-time ladder
text: The by-the-time ladder With 'by the time' and two past events, the earlier event takes had + V3 and the later one takes simple past. Put the blank on its step of the ladder. Fill in the Blanks

title: Three short verb lists
text: Three short verb lists Learn three lists. -ing after: avoid, enjoy, mind, suggest, finish. to + verb after: decide, hope, refuse, plan. Plain verb after: had better, would rather, let, make. Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Writing 'to hear' after 'look forward to'.
title.right: That 'to' is a preposition: look forward to hearing.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Using the present perfect with a finished time (has gone yesterday).
title.right: With yesterday, last week or in 2010, use the simple past: went.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Writing 'used to + -ing' for a past habit.
title.right: Past habit = used to + V1 (used to swim). Be used to + -ing means 'accustomed'.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Putting 'will' in the if-part of a type 1 sentence.
title.right: If + simple present, will + V1: If it rains, we will stay.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Making the verb agree with the nearest plural noun after 'each of'.
title.right: Each of / neither of + plural noun still takes a singular verb.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Using an active form when the subject receives the action.
title.right: Use the passive: the building had been evacuated.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title: Connective and relative-pronoun blanks — Fill in the Blanks
text: Connective and relative-pronoun blanks No sooner ... than / Hardly ... when Relative pronoun (who / whom / whose / which) Contrast and cause words Possessive and reflexive pronouns despite / although: check what follows however / therefore / moreover / otherwise lest ... should A connective is a joining word like although , because or therefore . The blank asks how two parts of a sentence are linked: contrast, cause, result, addition or time. Relative pronouns like who , whom and which join a describing part to a noun.

title: Find the other half of the pair
text: Find the other half of the pair Scan the sentence for the first half of a pair. 'Hardly had' fixes the blank as 'when'. 'No sooner had' fixes it as 'than'. Fill in the Blanks

title: He / him test for who / whom
text: He / him test for who / whom Rewrite the clause as a sentence. If 'he' fits, use who. If 'him' fits, use whom. Fill in the Blanks

title: Clause or noun after the blank?
text: Clause or noun after the blank? A full clause (subject + verb) after the blank needs although / though. A noun or -ing form needs despite / in spite of. Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Choosing 'than' after Hardly or Scarcely.
title.right: Hardly / Scarcely go with 'when'; only No sooner goes with 'than'.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Using 'whom' as the subject of the clause ('the man whom came').
title.right: The subject of the clause is 'who': the man who came.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Putting a full clause after 'despite' or a bare noun after 'although'.
title.right: despite + noun (despite the rain); although + clause (although it rained).

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Using 'which' for a person or 'who' for a thing.
title.right: who / whom for people; which / that for things.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Using 'that' after a comma.
title.right: After a comma, use which (things) or who (people).

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title: Confusable and homonym blanks — Fill in the Blanks
text: Confusable and homonym blanks Noun and verb twins (-ce / -se) lose / loose and affect / effect stationary / stationery and principal / principle censure / censor and allusion / illusion assure / ensure / insure continual / continuous and practical / practicable beside / besides and lie / lay Some words look or sound almost the same but mean different things, like advice and advise . The options give you such a pair or group. First find what kind of word the blank needs (noun, verb or adjective). Then choose by meaning.

title: Word type first, meaning second
text: Word type first, meaning second Decide noun, verb or adjective from the sentence. Remove every option of the wrong type. Usually only two options are left for the meaning check. Fill in the Blanks

title: Picture the sentence
text: Picture the sentence Make a quick mental picture. A shop full of paper and pens → stationery. A parked van → stationary. Fill in the Blanks

title: Learn the groups of three
text: Learn the groups of three Make flash cards for groups: assure / ensure / insure, site / sight / cite, allusion / illusion / elusion. These appear together in options. Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Choosing the more familiar 'affect' when the slot needs a noun.
title.right: After a / an / the, use the noun 'effect'.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Treating advice and advise as the same word.
title.right: advice = noun, advise = verb. Check the slot.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Picking 'illegible' when the sentence is about being qualified.
title.right: Qualified = eligible. Illegible = cannot be read.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Missing that the sentence already has its verb.
title.right: If the verb is already there, the blank is usually a noun.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Choosing a form that does not exist, such as 'advices'.
title.right: Advice has no plural. Remove non-standard forms first.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title: Double blanks: two gaps, one sentence — Fill in the Blanks
text: Double blanks: two gaps, one sentence Both / either / neither pairs Two-word fixed expressions from ... to and between ... and No sooner ... than / Hardly ... when too ... to and so ... that Two content words with a contrast or link Some questions have two blanks in one sentence. Each option gives a pair of words, one for each blank. Fill the easier blank first. The wrong pairs then drop out, and you test the last one or two pairs in both blanks.

title: Spot the structure
text: Spot the structure Learn the skeletons: too + adjective + to + V1; so + adjective + that + clause; such + noun + that + clause; hardly ... when; no sooner ... than. Once you see the skeleton, both blanks fill at once. Fill in the Blanks

title: Let the verb decide
text: Let the verb decide Plural verb with two subjects → Both ... and. Singular verb → Either ... or / Neither ... nor, agreeing with the nearer noun. Fill in the Blanks

title: Learn fixed expressions in pairs
text: Learn fixed expressions in pairs Revise safe and sound, part and parcel, null and void, first and foremost, ways and means together. Options often join a real first half to a wrong second half. Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Solving the hard blank first.
title.right: Start with the blank that has a fixed partner or an obvious answer.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Choosing 'so ... that' when a plain verb follows the second blank.
title.right: A plain verb after the blank needs 'too ... to'.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Using 'Both ... and' with a singular verb.
title.right: Both ... and takes a plural verb; neither / either take the verb of the nearer subject.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Accepting a half-real expression such as 'part and half'.
title.right: Check both halves: the expression is 'part and parcel'.

text: [object Object] Fill in the Blanks

title.wrong: Stopping at the second blank.
title.right: Read to the full stop; the ending often confirms the meaning.

title: Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Grammar Essentials (Handbook) · English Language · Spot the error in a sentence · Verb form and tense blank · Improve the highlighted part · Question tags · Pick the correct sentence · Fixed preposition blank · Article blank (a / an / the) · Word form (noun / adjective / adverb) · Inversion and -ing / to forms

title: Parts of speech: nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Parts of speech: nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs Uncountable noun trap Word-form family choice Linking verb + adjective Pronoun case and owner many / much and fewer / less Look-alike adverbs and hardly Verb after news, police, cattle Possessive: 's or of Every word in a sentence does one of eight jobs. An error in grammar usually means a word is doing the wrong job. For example, a noun may stand where an adverb is needed. First find the job the slot needs. Then pick the word that does that job.

title: Cover the other name
text: Cover the other name When a pronoun sits next to a noun ( Ravi and I / Ravi and me ), cover the noun. Read the sentence with the pronoun alone. The form that sounds right is the answer. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Scan every noun
text: Scan every noun In an error-spotting sentence, circle each noun. Ask two questions. Can I count it? Is it one of the special groups (no plural, always plural, cattle-type)? Words like informations, furnitures and advices are favourite errors. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Few or a few: empty or half full
text: Few or a few: empty or half full Few and little mean the glass is nearly empty (a negative feeling). A few and a little mean there is something (a positive feeling). Let the rest of the sentence show the feeling. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Adjective order and word families
text: Adjective order and word families Adjectives follow the order OSASCOMP: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose. Example: a beautiful small old round brown Indian wooden table. Some adjectives have no degrees: unique, perfect, ideal, complete, entire, round, square, supreme, universal. So more unique is wrong. Learn word families: succeed, success, successful, successfully; courage, encourage, courageous; strength, strengthen, strong; beauty, beautify, beautiful; anger, angry, angrily. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Numbers with nouns
text: Numbers with nouns After a definite number, dozen, hundred, thousand, million, score, lakh, crore and pair take no -s: three dozen eggs, five hundred rupees . But dozens of eggs and hundreds of people keep the -s. A number + noun used as an adjective takes a hyphen and the noun stays singular: a five-year plan, a ten-rupee note, a two-hour delay . Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Where adverbs go
text: Where adverbs go Frequency words go before the main verb but after be : He always comes late. He is always late. Use very with the plain adjective and with -ing adjectives (very tall, very interesting). Use much with comparatives and many -ed words (much taller, much obliged). Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Making a no-plural noun plural: furnitures, informations, luggages, sceneries.
title.right: Keep it singular: furniture, information, luggage, scenery.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using myself as a subject: Ravi and myself will attend.
title.right: Use I: Ravi and I will attend.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Writing elder than.
title.right: With than, say older than: she is older than me.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using less with countable nouns: less mistakes.
title.right: Use fewer with countable nouns: fewer mistakes.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Adding a second negative to hardly or scarcely: I could not hardly breathe.
title.right: Hardly is already negative: I could hardly breathe.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Adding -s to dozen, hundred or lakh after a number: five hundreds rupees.
title.right: Keep it plain after a number: five hundred rupees.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Tenses and sequence of tenses — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Tenses and sequence of tenses Signal word fixes the tense No future in the time or if clause Past perfect for the earlier past action Perfect continuous with since / for It is time / since + simple past By the time State verbs stay simple A tense shows when an action happens and whether it is finished, running or earlier than another action. You do not need to chant all twelve names. You need to know which signal word asks for which form. Underline the signal word first, then choose the verb form.

title: Scan for the signal word
text: Scan for the signal word Underline the time signal before reading the options. Since or for gives a perfect tense. Yesterday, ago or last gives the simple past. By + future time gives the future perfect. When, if or as soon as with future meaning gives the simple present. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: No will after when or if
text: No will after when or if If a clause starts with when, if, unless, until or as soon as and talks about the future, remove will from that clause. Will stays in the main clause only. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using the present perfect with a past time word: has gone yesterday.
title.right: Use the simple past: went yesterday.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using will in an if or when clause: If it will rain.
title.right: Use the present: If it rains, we will stay in.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Writing since two years.
title.right: Since needs a start point; for needs a length: for two years, since 2022.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using a state verb in the -ing form: I am understanding the problem.
title.right: Use the simple form: I understand the problem.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Changing a universal truth to the past in reported speech: said that the earth moved round the sun.
title.right: Keep the present: said that the earth moves round the sun.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using the simple past for both of two past events.
title.right: Give the earlier event had + V3: The train had left before we reached.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Subject-verb agreement (all rules and exceptions) — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Subject-verb agreement (all rules and exceptions) Head noun before an 'of' phrase Each, every, one of: fixed singular Nearer subject for neither ... nor Collective nouns and special singular subjects A number of and the number of Half, some, all + of X The rich, and one of those who A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. That rule is easy. The trap is finding the real subject . Extra phrases often stand between the subject and its verb. Strike them out first.

title: Strike-through method
text: Strike-through method Draw a line through every phrase that starts with a preposition (of the boys, in the box, with his friends). Also strike every add-on phrase (as well as, along with, together with). What stays before the verb is the true subject. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Nearest subject for or / nor pairs
text: Nearest subject for or / nor pairs For either ... or, neither ... nor, not only ... but also, or and nor, look only at the subject next to the verb. Put the plural subject second so the plural verb sounds natural. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: The number and a number
text: The number and a number The number is one figure, so it is singular. A number means many, so it is plural. Memory hook: A = Abundant. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Matching the verb with the noun just before it: The list of items are ready.
title.right: Match the head noun: The list of items is ready.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Treating as well as or along with like and, and using a plural verb.
title.right: The verb agrees with the first subject: The principal, as well as the teachers, was present.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using a plural verb after each, every, either or neither.
title.right: Use a singular verb: Each of the girls was given a prize.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using a singular verb after one of those who.
title.right: The who-clause describes the whole group: one of those people who never give up.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Treating people, police and cattle as singular.
title.right: They take a plural verb: The police are here.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using a plural verb for a sum of money or a distance treated as one amount.
title.right: Use a singular verb: Fifty rupees is too much.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Articles (a, an, the, zero article) and determiners — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Articles (a, an, the, zero article) and determiners A or an by first sound Compulsory the Zero article traps Few / a few, little / a little Article before a rate or a fixed phrase Geographical names Each, every, some, any Articles are the small words a, an and the. Choose a or an by the first sound of the next word, not by its spelling. Use the for a particular or unique thing. Some nouns take no article at all. Small words like few, little, each and every are determiners and also decide marks.

title: Say it aloud
text: Say it aloud For a or an, whisper the next word. A vowel sound (on-est, em-el-ay, ex-ray) needs an . A y or w sound (you-niversity, won-day) needs a . Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: The geography rule of thumb
text: The geography rule of thumb Plural names, water and chains take the : the Alps, the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Andamans. A single peak, a single lake, a city or most countries take no article: Mount Abu, Lake Dal, Delhi, Nepal. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Choosing a or an by spelling: an university, a hour, an European.
title.right: Go by sound: a university, an hour, a European.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using the with meals, games and languages: play the cricket, the English is easy.
title.right: Leave out the: play cricket, English is easy.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Dropping the before superlatives or same and only.
title.right: Use the: the best, the same, the only.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using the with a single mountain or lake: the Mount Everest.
title.right: Use no article: Mount Everest.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Leaving out a in rates and fixed phrases: twice week, in hurry.
title.right: Write: twice a week, in a hurry.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Prepositions and conjunctions — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Prepositions and conjunctions at / on / in for time and place Fixed preposition after a word Between / among and since / for Joining pairs No preposition after the verb Latin comparatives with to Two conjunctions for one job A preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence. A conjunction joins words or clauses. Most questions test fixed pairs, like fond of or no sooner ... than . You cannot work these out by logic. Learn them as pairs and match the partner.

title: Find the partner
text: Find the partner When you see hardly, scarcely, no sooner, not only, neither, either, both, whether, lest or though, look ahead for its fixed partner. A wrong or missing partner is very often the error. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Group prepositions by meaning
text: Group prepositions by meaning Stopping: prevent, refrain, abstain, desist from . Dependence: depend, rely, count on . Skill: good, expert, adept at ; proficient in . Latin comparatives: senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer to . One group takes one preposition. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Adding a preposition after discuss, reach, enter, resemble, request or comprise.
title.right: Use no preposition: discuss the plan, reach the station.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using between for more than two people or things.
title.right: Use among for more than two: among the villagers.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Writing prefer X than Y.
title.right: Write prefer X to Y.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using though ... but, because ... so or both ... as well as.
title.right: Use one conjunction, or the true pair: both ... and.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Adding not after unless, lest or until.
title.right: These words already carry a negative: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Using since with a length of time: since three days.
title.right: Use for with a length: for three days.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Modals, conditionals and the subjunctive — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Modals, conditionals and the subjunctive Modal + base form Shades of meaning Modal + have + V3 Conditional tense matching Unless and inverted conditionals Wish and as if Need, dare and used to Modal verbs like can, may, must and should add a shade of meaning to the main verb. A conditional sentence joins an if clause to a result clause. The exam tests two things: the form after a modal, and the matching of tenses in a conditional.

title: Match the type by the if-clause
text: Match the type by the if-clause Read only the if-clause. Present simple: use will or can in the result. Past simple: use would in the result. Past perfect: use would have + V3. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Modal + base form
text: Modal + base form After any modal the next verb is bare. If you see a modal followed by to, -s, -ing or -ed, that is the error. The only exceptions are ought to and used to. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: She can sings well.
title.right: She can sing well. A modal takes the base form.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: You must to go now.
title.right: You must go now.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay home.
title.right: If it rains, we will stay home.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: If I would have money, I would buy a car.
title.right: If I had money, I would buy a car.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: If I was you, I would apologise.
title.right: If I were you, I would apologise.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
title.right: Unless you work hard, you will fail.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: You needn't to come.
title.right: You needn't come.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Degrees of comparison and question tags — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Degrees of comparison and question tags Double comparative or superlative Than, to, and like with like Any other and superlative sense Question tag polarity Special tag cases Elder / older, later / latter, farther / further Positive, comparative, superlative conversion Adjectives and adverbs have three degrees: positive, comparative and superlative. A question tag is the short question added to a statement, like isn't it? . Both follow strict patterns, so learn the pattern and check it.

title: Flip the polarity
text: Flip the polarity Read the statement. Note whether it is positive or negative. Then use the helper verb with the opposite sign and a pronoun. Command? Use will you. Let's? Use shall we. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Watch than, that of and other
text: Watch than, that of and other When a comparison feels odd, check two things. First: are two like things compared (use that of or those of )? Second: does the comparison come from the same group (add other )? Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: She is more cleverer than her sister.
title.right: She is cleverer than her sister.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: This is the most best book.
title.right: This is the best book.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: He is taller than any boy in the class.
title.right: He is taller than any other boy in the class.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: The climate of Goa is better than Delhi.
title.right: The climate of Goa is better than that of Delhi.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: He is senior than me.
title.right: He is senior to me.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Nobody came, didn't they?
title.right: Nobody came, did they?

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: I am late, amn't I?
title.right: I am late, aren't I?

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Non-finites (infinitive, gerund, participle), inversion and parallelism — Grammar Essentials (Handbook)
text: Non-finites (infinitive, gerund, participle), inversion and parallelism Verb + infinitive or gerund Preposition + gerund Dangling participles Inversion after negative openers Bare infinitive after let, make, see, hear Stop, remember, forget, try So, neither and nor agreement Non-finite verb forms are the infinitive (to go), the gerund (going) and the participle (going, gone). They do not show tense or number by themselves. Inversion means putting the helper verb before the subject, as in questions and after some negative words.

title: Preposition then -ing
text: Preposition then -ing If the word before the blank is a preposition (of, in, at, without, after, before, by, about), the verb must end in -ing. Watch for to in look forward to and used to: it is a preposition there. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title: Negative start means flip
text: Negative start means flip When a sentence opens with never, rarely, hardly, no sooner, not only or not until, flip the first helper before the subject. If there is no helper, add do, does or did. Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: She enjoys to dance.
title.right: She enjoys dancing.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: He is interested to learn music.
title.right: He is interested in learning music.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: I look forward to meet you.
title.right: I look forward to meeting you.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Hardly he had left when it rained.
title.right: Hardly had he left when it rained.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Never I have seen such a crowd.
title.right: Never have I seen such a crowd.

text: [object Object] Grammar Essentials (Handbook)

title.wrong: Walking down the road, the rain began.
title.right: Walking down the road, I felt the rain begin.

title.right: She asked where he went.

title: Idioms & Phrases
text: Idioms & Phrases · English Language · Meaning of an idiom · Idiom inside a sentence · Animal and body-part idioms · Colour and food idioms · Fill the blank with an idiom · Idioms from stories · Replace the words with an idiom · Opposite of an idiom · Phrasal verbs

title: Why literal meaning is always wrong — and how to find the picture — Idioms & Phrases
text: Why literal meaning is always wrong — and how to find the picture Idiom with a literal decoy Idiom inside a sentence Close figurative trap Look-alike idiom pairs Tone check An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning is not the meaning of the separate words. The words paint a picture, and the meaning is what the picture stands for. The exam always plants a literal option, so cross it out first.

title: Photo test
text: Photo test If you could take a photo of what an option says, it is almost always wrong. This removes one option in nearly every question. Idioms & Phrases

title: Plug-back check
text: Plug-back check Put your chosen meaning into a sentence in place of the idiom. If the sentence sounds natural, keep it. Idioms & Phrases

title: Tone from the key word
text: Tone from the key word Cold, dark and hot often signal trouble. Cloud nine and red-letter signal joy. Use this when you do not know an idiom. Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Choosing the option that repeats the words of the idiom.
title.right: Cross out any option you could photograph. It is a literal decoy.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Learning an idiom by its words but not its picture.
title.right: Learn the picture and what it stands for.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Ignoring the tone of the idiom.
title.right: Say if it is happy, sad or angry. Pick the same tone.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Matching on one shared word (beans, milk).
title.right: Look-alike idioms share a word but not a meaning. Learn them in pairs.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Skipping the sentence in a context question.
title.right: Let the situation in the sentence fix the meaning.
