title: Animal and body-part idioms — Idioms & Phrases
text: Animal and body-part idioms Animal idiom meaning Body-part idiom meaning Animal or body idiom in a sentence Choose the idiom for a meaning Playful or hostile trap Many exam idioms use an animal or a body part. Each animal has a fixed character and each body part a fixed job. Use that to work out an idiom even when you half remember it.

title: Character first
text: Character first Name the animal or body part, then recall its character or job. The meaning usually follows. Idioms & Phrases

title: Body parts in sets
text: Body parts in sets Learn hand idioms together: lend a hand, have your hands full, wash your hands of. The job is help or work. Idioms & Phrases

title: One card for opaque idioms
text: One card for opaque idioms Write a card for each idiom whose picture is hard to see. Read those cards first in revision. Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading pull someone's leg as hurting someone.
title.right: It means to tease playfully.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading cold shoulder as an illness.
title.right: It means to treat someone coldly.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Mixing smell a rat with the rat race.
title.right: Smell a rat means suspect a trick. The rat race is a tiring fight for success.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading heart in your mouth as love.
title.right: It means extreme fear or nervousness.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading wash your hands of as cleanliness.
title.right: It means to refuse any more responsibility.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title: Colour and food idioms — Idioms & Phrases
text: Colour and food idioms Colour idiom meaning Food idiom meaning Look-alike twin Fill the blank with an idiom Choose the idiom for a meaning In English idioms each colour carries a feeling, and food is used to judge a task or a person. Learn the colour or food and you know the family of the meaning. Watch the look-alike pairs, such as red tape and red-letter day.

title: Colour to feeling
text: Colour to feeling Say the colour and its feeling before you read the options. Blue means sudden or rare, and the options then sort themselves. Idioms & Phrases

title: Food gives a verdict
text: Food gives a verdict Ask what verdict the food gives: easy, hard, flattery or trouble. That is the meaning. Idioms & Phrases

title: Pair cards
text: Pair cards Write the twins on one card: red tape and red-letter day, apple of the eye and apple of discord. Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Mixing red tape with a red-letter day.
title.right: Red tape is delay. A red-letter day is a happy day.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Mixing the apple of one's eye with the apple of discord.
title.right: The first is most loved. The second is a cause of a quarrel.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading a food idiom literally (a piece of cake as a treat).
title.right: Food idioms judge a task or a person. Cake means easy.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Filling a blank without checking the grammar.
title.right: After was, choose a noun phrase such as a red-letter day.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Learning colours without their feelings.
title.right: Learn the feeling: blue unexpected, green envy, black disgrace.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title: Idioms for situations and types of people — Idioms & Phrases
text: Idioms for situations and types of people Situation idiom meaning People idiom meaning Fill the blank with a situation idiom Idioms from stories Bad to worse and blame idioms Many idioms describe situations, such as trouble, effort or suddenness, and types of people, such as false, weak or reliable. Sort each idiom into a family and the right option stands out. A few idioms come from old stories, and one line of the story gives the meaning.

title: Family first
text: Family first Name the family of the situation before you read the options. Effort, trouble and suddenness cover a large share. Idioms & Phrases

title: One line per story
text: One line per story Store each story idiom as one line: Achilles, heel, weak point. Do not learn the whole story. Idioms & Phrases

title: Read the whole sentence
text: Read the whole sentence In a blank question, say what the person does. Escape means took to his heels. Hard work means burnt the midnight oil. Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading pass the buck as passing money.
title.right: It means to shift blame or duty to someone else.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading steal a march on as stealing.
title.right: It means to gain an advantage over someone.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading under the weather as being in the rain.
title.right: It means slightly ill.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading play second fiddle as music.
title.right: It means to accept a lower role.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Guessing a story idiom without the story.
title.right: Recall the one-line story and turn it into a meaning.

title: Phrasal verbs (verb + particle phrases) — Idioms & Phrases
text: Phrasal verbs (verb + particle phrases) Meaning of a phrasal verb Fill in the particle Same verb, different particles Replace a formal word Three-word phrasal verb A phrasal verb is a verb joined with a small word called a particle, such as up, off, out or in. Together they give a new meaning, like give up, which means stop. They appear in idiom questions, fill-in-the-blank and error spotting.

title: Swap for one word
text: Swap for one word Replace the phrasal verb with one plain word, such as cancel, refuse or tolerate. Test it in the sentence. Idioms & Phrases

title: Subject shows the particle
text: Subject shows the particle A car breaks down. A fire breaks out. A thief breaks in. The subject picks the particle. Idioms & Phrases

title: Learn by verb
text: Learn by verb Learn one verb with all its particles in one sitting: give up, give in, give away, give out. Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Guessing a phrasal verb from the verb alone.
title.right: The particle changes the meaning. Learn the whole phrase.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Mixing put off and put out.
title.right: Put off means postpone. Put out means extinguish.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Writing 'run out sugar'.
title.right: Write 'run out of sugar'. Keep both particles.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Mixing break down, break out and break in.
title.right: Down means stop working. Out means start suddenly. In means enter by force.

text: [object Object] Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Learning particles as strict rules.
title.right: They are tendencies. Learn each common phrase with its meaning.

title: Exam strategy: banking 300 idioms in 30 days — Idioms & Phrases
text: Exam strategy: banking 300 idioms in 30 days Complete the idiom Replace the phrase with an idiom Idiom from any family with a tone check Opposite in meaning to an idiom Frozen wording in a proverb Idioms are a small but steady part of the English section. The pool is small and repeats often, so a bank of about 300 idioms covers most papers. Learn in a 30-day plan and use your own sentences.

title: Own sentence
text: Own sentence Write one sentence of your own for each idiom. The sentence is what you remember under pressure. Idioms & Phrases

title: Format first
text: Format first Name the format before you start. Meaning, replace, complete or opposite. Each has its own first step. Idioms & Phrases

title: Same-meaning trap
text: Same-meaning trap In an opposite question, the option with the same meaning as the idiom is always wrong. Idioms & Phrases

title.wrong: Reading a list of idioms once.
title.right: Write one sentence of your own for each idiom.

title.right: Idioms are frozen. Learn the exact words.

title.right: Write the meaning first, then reverse it.

title.right: Learn by family so the clusters help recall.

title: One Word Substitution
text: One Word Substitution · English Language · One who ... (person words) · Killing words (-cide) · Fear and study words · A place where ... / A group of ... · Government words (-cracy / -archy) · Writing and speech words · Medical words · Correctly spelt substitute

title: Suffix families: decode the word by its ending — One Word Substitution
text: Suffix families: decode the word by its ending Killing words (-cide) Fear words (-phobia) Study words (-ology) Lover, eater and marriage words Counting-prefix words In one-word substitution you get a phrase and pick the single word for it. Many answer words are two parts: a root for the object and a suffix for the family. Learn the suffix and you can build the meaning of words you have not seen.

title: Family first, root second
text: Family first, root second Read the phrase and name the family (killing, fear, study). Then match the root. Two steps remove most options. One Word Substitution

title: Stack two families
text: Stack two families Rare words are often two parts joined. Nycto + phobia is fear of darkness. Entomo + logy is study of insects. One Word Substitution

title: Make look-alike cards
text: Make look-alike cards Write each look-alike pair on one card with the meaning of each word. Revise the cards every week. One Word Substitution

title.wrong: Memorising each word alone.
title.right: Learn the suffix family and the root. Build the word from two parts.

text: [object Object] One Word Substitution

title.wrong: Marking entomology for 'word origins'.
title.right: Entomology is insects. Etymology is word origins.

title.wrong: Mixing patricide, fratricide and matricide.
title.right: Father is pater, brother is frater, mother is mater. Check the victim.

text: [object Object] One Word Substitution

title.wrong: Confusing -phobia (fear) with -phile (love).
title.right: Phobia means fear. Phile means love.

title.wrong: Marking a word after reading only its ending.
title.right: Check the root as well. Options often share the same suffix.

title: One word for people: traits, trades and types — One Word Substitution
text: One word for people: traits, trades and types Person by job Person by habit or character Partner-word trap Root-built person words Look-alike person words Most one-word-substitution items start with 'One who' or 'A person who'. They name a person by a job, a habit, a feeling or a situation. Sort them into four boxes and watch out for the partner word planted as a trap.

title: Object first
text: Object first Underline the object or habit in the stem before you read the options. It names the family at once. One Word Substitution

title: Learn words in pairs
text: Learn words in pairs Take each word with its partner. Widow goes with widower. Miser goes with spendthrift. The pair is one memory item. One Word Substitution

title: Speak the parts
text: Speak the parts Say the parts aloud: somn, ambul, ist. Hearing the parts locks the meaning. One Word Substitution

title.wrong: Choosing astrologer for 'studies the stars scientifically'.

title.wrong: Ignoring the gender word (widow for a man).

title.wrong: Confusing miser and spendthrift.
title.right: Miser hoards money. Spendthrift wastes it.

title.wrong: Confusing polyglot and polymath.
title.right: Polyglot knows many languages. Polymath knows many subjects.

title.wrong: Learning words without the object.

title: One word for places and groups — One Word Substitution
text: One word for places and groups Place where something is kept or made Place named by the people in it Collective noun for animals Collective noun for things or people Look-alike place pairs Two question shapes are pure matching. 'A place where X is kept or done' needs a place word. 'A group of X' needs a collective noun. Find the key noun in the phrase and recall its partner.

title: Animal decides the group
text: Animal decides the group Name the animal in the phrase first. Then recall its one group word. One Word Substitution

title: Sound hooks
text: Sound hooks Link each look-alike to a sound: api sounds like ape-bee, avi is in aviation. Hooks beat plain rote. One Word Substitution

title: Twenty and twenty
text: Twenty and twenty About twenty place words and twenty group words cover nearly every paper. Learn them in one sitting and revise once a week. One Word Substitution

title.wrong: Mixing apiary and aviary.
title.right: Api goes with bees. Avi goes with aviation and birds.

title.right: Kept is mortuary. Buried is cemetery.

title.wrong: Swapping monastery and convent.
title.right: Monks live in a monastery. Nuns live in a convent.

title.wrong: Using the wrong group word (herd for lions).
title.right: Name the animal first. Lions form a pride.

title: Exam strategy for one-word substitution — One Word Substitution
text: Exam strategy for one-word substitution Specific word beats the general word Medical and science words Correctly spelt substitute Direction and contrast pairs Classify, then remove families One-word substitution gives one or two quick marks in most papers. It is a memory topic, so the plan is to build a word bank by category and revise it every week. In the exam, classify the phrase, remove other families, and prefer the more specific word.

title: Specific beats general
text: Specific beats general If both a general and a specific word fit, choose the specific one. It matches the detail the examiner gave. One Word Substitution

title: Weekly weak list
text: Weekly weak list Any word missed twice goes on a short list. Read only that list twice a week. One Word Substitution

title: Syllable check for spelling
text: Syllable check for spelling For spelling items say the word slowly in syllables and match each syllable to the option. One Word Substitution

title.wrong: Learning words in one long alphabet list.
title.right: Learn by category and keep a personal sheet.

title: Paragraph summary (main-idea questions) — Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion
text: Paragraph summary (main-idea questions) Best summary of the paragraph Author's argument in one line Which option is NOT supported Best title A summary question gives you a short paragraph and four candidate summaries. The right answer states the main idea in the same scope as the paragraph — nothing more, nothing less. Three things break a summary: it is too narrow (only one detail), too broad (claims more than the paragr

title: Find the topic sentence first
text: Find the topic sentence first Most exam paragraphs put the main idea in the first or last sentence. Mark it before reading the options — the correct summary will be a tighter version of that sentence. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: The every-word test
text: The every-word test Read the option and ask: does the paragraph support every claim in this sentence? One unsupported word ("always", "only", "the government must") disqualifies it. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Cut the extremes
text: Cut the extremes Options with strongest words — always, never, only, must, prove — are usually wrong summaries. Real authors hedge; good summaries hedge too. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Picking the summary of one example or statistic from the middle of the paragraph — that is a detail, not the main idea.
text: Picking the summary of one example or statistic from the middle of the paragraph — that is a detail, not the main idea. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Choosing an option because it uses the same words as the paragraph; wrong options often copy words but swap the claim.
text: Choosing an option because it uses the same words as the paragraph; wrong options often copy words but swap the claim. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Letting your own opinion fill the gap — the summary must contain only what the author said.
text: Letting your own opinion fill the gap — the summary must contain only what the author said. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Odd sentence out — Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion
text: Odd sentence out Topic-mate intruder Scope shift Time or place shift Direction shift (broken chain) You get four or five sentences that mostly build one theme, and one sentence that does not belong. The odd sentence usually shares some words with the theme — that is the trap. Test what the sentences do , not what they mention: the theme is an idea (a cause, a process, a place, an event), an

title: Name the theme in 3 words
text: Name the theme in 3 words After reading all sentences, say the theme in three words (e.g. "mangroves protect coasts"). Any sentence that is not doing exactly that job is the odd one. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Watch the scope shift
text: Watch the scope shift The intruder often stays on-topic but shifts level: the paragraph is about a national programme and the odd sentence talks about one person's profit, or vice versa. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Check time and place anchors
text: Check time and place anchors If four sentences live in one time period or one place and one floats to another era or region for no reason, that one is out. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Picking the sentence with the rarest word instead of the sentence that breaks the theme's job.
text: Picking the sentence with the rarest word instead of the sentence that breaks the theme's job. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Keeping a sentence that merely mentions the theme's topic but actually develops a different point.
text: Keeping a sentence that merely mentions the theme's topic but actually develops a different point. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Choosing an odd sentence that is simply harder to understand — difficulty is not the test; relevance is.
text: Choosing an odd sentence that is simply harder to understand — difficulty is not the test; relevance is. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Paragraph completion — Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion
text: Paragraph completion Takeaway closer Cause–effect finisher Contrast resolution Continuation into detail A paragraph stops one step short of its natural end, and you must choose the sentence that completes it. The right closer does two things: it continues the last thought (no jump), and it finishes the paragraph's job (if the paragraph set up a problem, the closer points at the resolution; if

title: Predict before you peek
text: Predict before you peek Cover the options and finish the paragraph in your own words. Then pick the option closest to your prediction. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Match the direction of the last sentence
text: Match the direction of the last sentence If the last sentence turns negative (a problem), the closer usually completes that problem or its fix — it should not suddenly turn cheerful unless a contrast word appears. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: No new characters or claims
text: No new characters or claims The closer may reuse the paragraph's ideas but must not introduce a fresh actor, statistic, or recommendation out of nowhere. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Choosing a sentence that is true and pleasant but belongs to a different paragraph.
text: Choosing a sentence that is true and pleasant but belongs to a different paragraph. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Picking an option that merely restates the first sentence instead of moving the thought to its end.
text: Picking an option that merely restates the first sentence instead of moving the thought to its end. Paragraph Summary, Odd Sentence & Completion

title: Reading Comprehension
text: Reading Comprehension · English Language · Main idea of the passage · Best title · Fact question ('According to the passage') · NOT / EXCEPT question · Inference question · Meaning of a word in context · Author's tone · Structure and purpose questions

title: How to attempt an RC passage in SSC exams — Reading Comprehension
text: How to attempt an RC passage in SSC exams Statement combination (Which of statements I, II, III is true?) Purpose or role of a paragraph Why does the author mention X? (function of an example) How is the passage organised? (structure) Which question can be answered from the passage? Turning-point question (what comes after 'however'?) A reading passage in an SSC paper has 250 to 350 words and 5 questions. You get about 6 to 8 minutes for the whole set. Speed comes from a fixed routine, not from reading faster. Read the passage once, read the questions, then go back to the exact lines. Every answer must be written in the passage.

title: Two-minute structure read
text: Two-minute structure read On the first read, do not hunt for facts. After each paragraph, say its job in three words. Facts are easy to find again. Structure is what saves time. Reading Comprehension

title: Vocabulary first, main idea last
text: Vocabulary first, main idea last Answer the replace-the-word question and the line-specific details before the main-idea question. By then you have touched half the passage and the theme is clear. Reading Comprehension

title: Line anchoring
text: Line anchoring Every detail question has a home line. Match a distinctive word from the question (a name, a number, an odd noun) to the passage. Read two lines around it. Choose the option that paraphrases those lines. Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Answering from general knowledge because the option sounds true in real life.
title.right: Choose only what the passage says. Point to the line.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Spending four minutes on the first read to understand everything.
title.right: Use the first read only to map the passage. It should take about 2 minutes.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Leaving reading comprehension for the last two minutes.
title.right: The 5-question set is a high-value block. Give it a planned slot.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Choosing an option because it copies words from the passage.
title.right: Check that the meaning matches too. Copied words with a changed meaning are a trap.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Studying all four options before reading the passage.
title.right: Read the passage first, then only the question lines.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title: Main idea, central theme and best-title questions — Reading Comprehension
text: Main idea, central theme and best-title questions Central idea or main theme of the passage Most suitable title Author's primary purpose Main point of one paragraph or best summary What would the author discuss next? The main idea is the one big point the whole passage makes. The author keeps coming back to it. A title is the main idea squeezed into a short heading. The purpose is why the author wrote the passage. Check every option for three faults: too narrow, too broad and too extreme.

title: First and last sentence sketch
text: First and last sentence sketch Read the opening and closing sentences of the passage, plus the first sentence of each middle paragraph. This skeleton usually states or implies the theme. Build your ten-word summary from it before you read the options. Reading Comprehension

title: Count the mentions
text: Count the mentions The idea the author repeats in different words across paragraphs is the theme. If an option's core idea appears in only one paragraph, it is a detail, not the theme. Reading Comprehension

title: Title versus theme wording
text: Title versus theme wording Titles are noun phrases. Theme options are full claims. Judge both by scope, not by grammar. Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Picking a title that names only the first paragraph's example.
title.right: Pick the title that covers the whole passage.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Choosing the broadest-sounding option.
title.right: An option with no support in the passage is a trap, not a strength.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Confusing the author's closing suggestion with the theme.
title.right: A suggestion supports the idea. It is not the whole idea.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Selecting an option because its words appear in the passage.
title.right: Theme options paraphrase. Check the meaning, not the words.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title: Factual detail questions ('According to the passage…') — Reading Comprehension
text: Factual detail questions ('According to the passage…') Direct detail ('According to the passage...') Reason or cause detail ('Why...?') NOT mentioned or EXCEPT Which statement is true? (qualifiers and numbers) Complete the statement using the passage Detail questions ask what the passage says, line by line. The answer is written in the passage. The options paraphrase it, and the wrong options are built around it. Use the method: locate a keyword, read around it, say the answer in your own words, then match.

title: Paraphrase before you look
text: Paraphrase before you look After you locate the line, cover the options and answer in your own words. Then uncover and match. Reading Comprehension

title: Reversal scan
text: Reversal scan Before you mark a detail option, check its direction words: only, always, all, may, often, some, can, cannot. Wrong options flip these while keeping the same topic words. Reading Comprehension

title: Option pairing
text: Option pairing When two options say the same thing in different words, both are wrong. A fact has one meaning. Remove the pair, then judge the other two. Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Stopping at the line with the keyword.
title.right: Read one sentence before and after. The answer may be in the next sentence.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Choosing an option because it sounds authoritative, such as 'studies show...'.
title.right: Pick it only if the passage cites that study.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Missing NOT or EXCEPT in the stem and marking the true statement.
title.right: Circle NOT or EXCEPT first. The answer is the odd one out.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Ignoring qualifiers like mainly, only and some.
title.right: Compare every qualifier with the passage. Detail questions turn on these words.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title: Inference and extrapolation questions — Reading Comprehension
text: Inference and extrapolation questions 'It can be inferred from the passage that...' Implied meaning of a quoted line Assumption behind a statement Prediction or application (most likely, most similar) Which statement cannot be concluded? To infer is to reach a conclusion from clues. The passage does not say it in words, but it clearly suggests it. A detail is written on the page. An inference is one small step beyond the page. Use the must-be-true test: if the option were false, the passage would stop making sense.

title: One-step rule
text: One-step rule Correct inference = stated idea plus one logical step. Two steps, extra facts or a change of scale means reject. Reading Comprehension

title: Verbatim is a verdict
text: Verbatim is a verdict In an inference question, an option that repeats passage wording without adding a step is wrong by definition. Cross it out first. Reading Comprehension

title: Extremity filter
text: Extremity filter Inferences with only, never, must or inevitably are almost always one step too far. Moderate options (may, tends to, is likely) fit the must-be-true test better. Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Bringing in real-world facts to justify an option.
title.right: Use only what the passage supports.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Treating a copied line as an inference.
title.right: A copied line is a detail. An inference adds one step.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Inferring the author's personal life or politics from a neutral, informational passage.
title.right: Stay with what the text shows.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Choosing an inference so weak it could follow from any passage.
title.right: It must follow from this passage.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title: Vocabulary in context (replace-the-word / meaning questions) — Reading Comprehension
text: Vocabulary in context (replace-the-word / meaning questions) Synonym in context (closest meaning) Antonym in context (most nearly opposite) Meaning of a phrase or idiom in the passage Multiple-meaning word (which sense is used?) Unknown word: guess from the clues around it These questions give a word or phrase from the passage and ask its meaning as used there. Many English words have more than one meaning, and the sentence decides which one is right. Only one sentence matters, so do these questions first.

title: Own words first
text: Own words first Cover the options and replace the word with your own simple word. Then find the option that matches your word. This removes the dictionary-meaning bait. Reading Comprehension

title: Tone match
text: Tone match The substitute must keep the sentence's attitude. In a critical sentence, choose the critical option. A neutral synonym that drains the criticism is wrong. Reading Comprehension

title: Two-line rule for phrases
text: Two-line rule for phrases For phrase-meaning questions, read one line before and one line after. Figurative phrases get their meaning from the surrounding argument, not from the words. Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Picking the option with the word's most common meaning when the sentence needs another sense.
title.right: Test each option in the sentence. The sentence decides.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Changing the part of speech while plugging in, such as a noun option in a verb slot.
title.right: Keep the same part of speech as the passage word.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Choosing an opposite for an antonym question because it merely sounds negative.
title.right: Find the meaning first, then flip it once.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Reading five lines around the word.
title.right: Context questions need the sentence, or at most the sentence and its neighbour.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title: Tone, attitude and author's-opinion questions — Reading Comprehension
text: Tone, attitude and author's-opinion questions Tone of the passage Author's attitude towards a specific thing Author would agree or disagree with... Type or source of the passage Sarcasm or irony in a quoted line Tone questions ask how the author speaks, not what the author says. Tone is the author's feeling or manner. Attitude is the author's feeling towards one thing in the passage. Tone lives in adjectives, adverbs and contrast words, not in the facts themselves.

title: Adjective audit
text: Adjective audit Sweep the passage for adjectives and adverbs that carry feeling, such as quietly, badly, remarkable, merely, confident. Three of them in the same direction fix the tone. Reading Comprehension

title: However counts double
text: However counts double The clause after but, however or yet carries the author's real position. Tone and opinion questions key off the second half. Reading Comprehension

title: Degree matching
text: Degree matching Match intensity as well as direction. Pick the option at the same temperature as the passage. Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Calling a fact-heavy passage sarcastic because its subject is unpleasant.
title.right: Judge the author's words, not the subject. Facts only means informative.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Reading the tone of people quoted in the passage as the author's own tone.
title.right: Find the author's own evaluative words.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Choosing an extreme tone word such as outraged or euphoric when the passage argues in a moderate way.
title.right: Choose the option at the same strength as the passage.

text: [object Object] Reading Comprehension

title.wrong: Forgetting that a balanced or analytical option is often correct when the author gives both sides.
title.right: Check whether both sides are weighed before you pick a one-sided tone.

title: Sentence Improvement
text: Sentence Improvement · English Language · Tense fix · Agreement fix · Reported speech fix · Comparison fix · Preposition and repeated word fix · Article fix · Inversion fix · Misplaced opening phrase · When no change is needed

title: The elimination ladder: how to choose in 20 seconds — Sentence Improvement
text: The elimination ladder: how to choose in 20 seconds Single fault with repeat-fault decoys No substitution required Decoy families around the bold word Two-fault trap options Meaning guard between clean options In a sentence improvement question, one part of the sentence is in bold. Four options offer a replacement, and one of them is usually No substitution required . You are not looking for the best-sounding English. You are looking for the one option that passes every grammar test the bold part failed.

title: Find the anchor before you read the options
text: Find the anchor before you read the options Look for the time word or helper verb near the bold part. Decide what the verb must look like. Then pick the option that matches your form. Sentence Improvement

title: Tag every option with its flaw
text: Tag every option with its flaw In your head, label each option: 'plural verb', 'wrong partner', 'breaks inversion'. If no option has a flaw, the answer is No substitution required. Sentence Improvement

title: Meaning guard
text: Meaning guard Two options are both grammatical? Choose the one that keeps the original meaning word for word. An option that changes who did what is wrong. Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Choosing a correct option that changes the meaning (active to passive, an added doer).
title.right: Keep the meaning. Change only what the fault needs.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Choosing 'No substitution required' because the sentence sounds natural.
title.right: Run the tense, agreement and structure checks first.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Repairing a part that is not in bold.
title.right: Only the bold part may change.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Missing the anchor word outside the bold part.
title.right: Read the whole sentence before you look at the options.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Picking an option that fixes one fault and adds another.
title.right: Read the finished sentence again once.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title: Tense and sequence fixes — Sentence Improvement
text: Tense and sequence fixes Anchor-based tense fix Reported speech: backshift and order Conditional half repair Since / for with a continuing action Future meaning inside a when or until clause Many improvement questions bold a verb whose tense clashes with a word in plain sight, like yesterday , since or already . Find that word first. It tells you the tense. Then check the other verbs in the sentence, because tense is always about a pair of times.

title: The yesterday test
text: The yesterday test See a finished-time word? Cross out every perfect and continuous option at once. Usually one option is left. Sentence Improvement

title: Backshift plus straight order
text: Backshift plus straight order In a reported question, two things change: the tense moves back and the order becomes a statement. Each wrong option usually breaks one of these. Check both. Sentence Improvement

title: Since and for health check
text: Since and for health check 'Since 2015' or 'for ten years' with a continuing action needs 'has / have been'. Options without it die at once. Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Using the present perfect with 'yesterday' or 'last year' because it sounds formal.
title.right: A finished past time takes the simple past.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Backshifting the tense but keeping question order in reported speech.
title.right: Do both: 'asked why he was late'.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Changing a correct perfect to the simple past when 'since' or 'for' is present.
title.right: Keep has / have been for a continuing action.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Changing continuous to simple (or back) and altering the meaning.
title.right: Keep the meaning: was cooking is not the same as cooked.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Putting 'will' inside an if-clause or a when-clause.
title.right: Use the simple present there. 'Will' belongs to the main clause.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title: Agreement and verb-form fixes — Sentence Improvement
text: Agreement and verb-form fixes Phrase between subject and helper One of / each of / neither of Nearer-subject rule (or / nor / not only ... but also) Quantity phrase (a number of / many a) Two subjects joined by and When the bold part holds a verb, first find the real subject . Phrases like of the students or as well as the players often stand between the subject and the verb. They do not change the number of the verb.

title: Cover the phrase and read the skeleton
text: Cover the phrase and read the skeleton Cover 'of the students' type phrases with a finger. Read what is left: 'One ___ won'. The right helper is now easy. Sentence Improvement

title: Check the helper chain
text: Check the helper chain did takes the base verb, have takes the participle, be takes -ing or the participle. If the bold part has a helper, check its partner form first. Sentence Improvement

title: Two subjects with and
text: Two subjects with and Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb. The exception is a pair that names one thing, like 'bread and butter is'. Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Agreeing with the nearest noun instead of the real subject.
title.right: Cross out the of-phrase and find the head noun.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Writing a participle after 'did' (did he arrived).
title.right: After did, use the base verb: did he arrive.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Choosing an option that changes active to passive or adds a doer.
title.right: Fix only the helper. Keep the meaning.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Accepting a plural verb after 'each of the + plural noun'.
title.right: Each, one and neither stay singular.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Treating 'as well as' like 'and'.
title.right: As well as only adds information. It does not make the subject plural.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title: Comparison and structural fixes — Sentence Improvement
text: Comparison and structural fixes Double-marker fix That of / those of repair Latin comparative and prefer Count of items (two or more) Words that are already absolute Comparison questions test four things. These are a doubled marker ( more better ), unlike things compared, to after senior and its kin, and the count of items. The right option is usually the smallest change. An option that rewrites half the sentence is only there to distract you.

title: Insert that of or those of
text: Insert that of or those of Two 'the X of A' phrases are compared, but the second is bare. Add 'that of' for a singular noun or 'those of' for a plural noun. Sentence Improvement

title: Check for a double marker
text: Check for a double marker Look for more + a word that already has -er, or most + a word that already has -est. If you find one, the repair is a subtraction. Sentence Improvement

title: Count first
text: Count first Find the count phrase in the sentence. 'Of the two' means the comparative with 'the'. 'Of all' means the superlative. Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Choosing 'than that of' when the sentence does not compare two possessive phrases.
title.right: Use 'that of' or 'those of' only when unlike things are compared.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Fixing more better into more good.
title.right: Drop the extra marker. Say 'better'.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Writing 'senior than' or 'prefer X than Y'.
title.right: Say 'senior to' and 'prefer X to Y'.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Using the superlative when the sentence says 'of the two'.
title.right: Two items need the comparative with 'the': the more useful.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Treating 'No substitution required' as wrong because the sentence looks plain.
title.right: Plain and correct are different from wrong.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title: Precision fixes: articles, prepositions, pronouns, word choice — Sentence Improvement
text: Precision fixes: articles, prepositions, pronouns, word choice Preposition partner repair Article sound repair Redundancy cut Swapped twin repair Win / beat and say / tell Some bold parts have no verb. The fault is a wrong small word: an article, a preposition, a pronoun, or a word that repeats another. The options then differ by one or two words. Learn the fixed partners well, because meaning alone will pull you towards the wrong one.

title: Sweep the small words
text: Sweep the small words Read only the small words in the bold part: a, an, the, in, on, at, me, myself. A wrong one usually stands alone. Fix it and finish. Sentence Improvement

title: The myself firewall
text: The myself firewall A reflexive like 'myself' never replaces a plain object pronoun. Any option that offers 'myself' where 'me' belongs is a decoy. Sentence Improvement

title: Redundancy flinch
text: Redundancy flinch Learn the fatal pairs: return back, repeat again, revert back, final conclusion. When one is bold, the shorter option is the key. Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Judging a / an by spelling (a hour, an university).
title.right: Judge by sound: an hour, a university.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Choosing 'myself' as a polite word for 'me'.
title.right: Use 'me' as the object. 'Myself' needs the same person as the doer.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Changing few to a few (or back) without checking the meaning.
title.right: Few means hardly any. A few means some.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Writing 'despite of'.
title.right: Write 'despite' or 'in spite of'.

text: [object Object] Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Choosing a preposition by meaning alone.
title.right: Recall the fixed partner: approve of, insist on, fond of.

title: Structural fixes: inversion, dangling modifiers, parallelism — Sentence Improvement
text: Structural fixes: inversion, dangling modifiers, parallelism No sooner / hardly frame repair Negative adverb inversion Dangling modifier repair Parallel shape in lists and pairs Order inside a reported question Some bold parts fail in sentence shape, not in tense or agreement. Four shapes cover the exam: inversion after negative openers, dangling openers, matching shapes in lists and pairs, and statement order in reported questions. Each is a fixed pattern, so the right option is easy to spot once you know

title: Opener triggers a flip
text: Opener triggers a flip Negative word first? Expect helper before subject: had I reached, did he arrive. Then check the partner: than or when. Sentence Improvement

title: Who does the -ing?
text: Who does the -ing? Name the doer of the opening action. If the main subject is not that doer, pick the option that makes the doer the subject. Sentence Improvement

title: Shape match across pairs
text: Shape match across pairs Cover the pair words. Compare the shapes on both sides. If one side is a verb and the other a noun, that is the fault. Sentence Improvement

title.wrong: Inverting a clause that has no negative opener.
title.right: Invert only after openers like no sooner, hardly, never, seldom.

title.wrong: Pairing 'Hardly ... than' or 'No sooner ... when'.
title.right: No sooner goes with than. Hardly and scarcely go with when.

title.right: Make every item the same kind of word.

title: The PQRS method: label, anchor, chain, eliminate — Sentence Rearrangement
text: The PQRS method: label, anchor, chain, eliminate Argument skeleton (claim, support, turn, close) Problem skeleton (problem, cause, effect, response) S6 pull-back S1 hook Two-pair lock Name the broken link in each wrong string A PQRS question shows sentence 1 (S1) and sentence 6 (S6) in place. The four middle parts P, Q, R, S are mixed up. You choose the right order from four letter strings, such as QPSR . Do not test every string. Tag each part, find two strong links, and remove the strings that break them.

title: Pairs before strings
text: Pairs before strings Do not read the four strings first. Build two or three pairs from P, Q, R, S. Then see which strings keep them. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Frame test
text: Frame test After you chain the parts, read S1, your chain and S6 as one paragraph. If any it , this or they has no noun, the chain is wrong. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Adjacent-swap check
text: Adjacent-swap check Wrong strings usually swap two neighbours. Find the one swap in each wrong string and name the broken pair. That proves your answer. Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Reading all four strings against the whole paragraph.
title.right: Find two strong links first, then remove strings that break them.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Starting the chain with a pronoun part whose noun comes later.
title.right: Put the part that names the noun first.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Ignoring S6 when a middle part has *therefore* or *thus*.
title.right: That part usually sits just before S6.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Forcing the string you like.
title.right: Remove strings one broken link at a time.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Judging order by which part sounds nice alone.
title.right: Judge by links: pronouns, *a* to *the*, cause to effect.

title: Opening and closing sentence clues — Sentence Rearrangement
text: Opening and closing sentence clues Orphan test for the opener Connector follows the claim it turns on Closing signal part General before specific Hidden follow-on words (also, even, others) The first and last parts of a jumble are the easiest to find. A part cannot open if it holds a pronoun, a connector, or a the with no earlier mention. A part closes well if it gives a result, a lesson or a look ahead. Fix the ends first. Then the middle is short work.

title: Pronoun orphan test
text: Pronoun orphan test A part that starts with he, she, it, they, this or these needs its noun earlier. If a string gives no earlier noun, cross it out. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Connector ban
text: Connector ban But, However, Therefore, Thus and So cannot open a free jumble. Two of four options often start with such parts. Cross them out. In a PQRS item, check whether S1 is the claim first. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Ask what comes before S6
text: Ask what comes before S6 Read S6 and ask which sentence must come just before it. It is often the part with Thus , That is why or a summing-up judgement. Pin it, then build backwards. Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Opening with a *the* sentence whose noun appears nowhere before it.
title.right: Open with the part that introduces the noun with *a* or a plain noun phrase.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Treating a general claim and its example as interchangeable.
title.right: Put the general claim first and the example after it.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Missing that *Now* signals a present-time contrast.
title.right: Place it after the past-time claim it contrasts.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Putting *Thus...* in the middle of the chain.
title.right: Put the concluding part last, before S6.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Banning every connector part from the front, even in a PQRS item.
title.right: Check S1. A connector can follow S1 directly when S1 is the claim it turns on.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title: Mandatory pairs: the links that never break — Sentence Rearrangement
text: Mandatory pairs: the links that never break Noun to pronoun or place-word pair A to the pair This or these plus an abstract noun Contrast pair (claim, then but, yet, however) Question to answer pair Hidden pointers (others, even, also) A mandatory pair is two parts that must sit next to each other. Examples are a noun and its pronoun, or a and the later the . Most items are solved by finding two or three such pairs. Trust the strongest link first.

title: Noun-first scan
text: Noun-first scan List the nouns and pronouns in P, Q, R, S. Circle each pronoun and each the noun. Draw an arrow to the part that brings in its noun. The arrows are the answer skeleton. Sentence Rearrangement

title: This + noun hunt
text: This + noun hunt For every this + abstract noun , find the part that holds that idea. The order is then forced. Sentence Rearrangement

title: A-to-the cascade
text: A-to-the cascade The part with a + noun comes before every part with the + same noun . This orders many food and story passages at once. Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Breaking a noun-to-pronoun pair to fit a time marker.
title.right: Keep the pronoun pair. It is a stronger link.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Missing the second mention of a noun (*the bread* after *a piece of bread*).
title.right: Scan every part for repeated nouns.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Placing an effect before its cause because the cause reads well alone.
title.right: Put *This*, *As a result* and *Therefore* parts after the cause.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Ignoring number in a pronoun chain (*its* for *workers*).
title.right: Match gender and number: *its* for one thing, *their* for many.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Linking two parts only because they share a topic.
title.right: Use grammar links: pronoun, *a* to *the*, *this + noun*, connector.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title: Time-sequence chains — Sentence Rearrangement
text: Time-sequence chains Explicit time and date markers By-phrases and day boundaries Tense as a clock (past perfect flashback) Process steps Biography with pointer words Story and history jumbles follow the clock. Use time words first, then tenses, then cause and effect. Number the events in order, and the letter string writes itself.

title: Timeline first
text: Timeline first Write the four to six events as a numbered list. Then map the numbers to the letters. The string writes itself. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Tense radar
text: Tense radar Past perfect is earlier. Past continuous is background. Simple past is the main story line. Use tense when time words are missing. Sentence Rearrangement

title: By-time capping
text: By-time capping By midnight and By dawn close the phase they describe. They follow the event chain and never open it. Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Placing *Now* or *Today* early in a story that ends in the present.
title.right: Put present-time parts last.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Ordering the parts by how they are listed.
title.right: Order them by when the events happened.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Ignoring *The next morning*.
title.right: Treat it as a day boundary. Put it after everything from the day before.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Letting a result-time phrase such as *By dawn* open the chain.
title.right: Put it after the actions it sums up.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Putting a past-perfect flashback after the event it explains.
title.right: Keep flashback parts together, straight after the scene.

title: Exam strategy: elimination, budget and Tier 2 jumbles — Sentence Rearrangement
text: Exam strategy: elimination, budget and Tier 2 jumbles Paragraph jumble with no fixed ends Which sentence comes first? Which sentence comes last? Two strings left: test only the difference Odd sentence out Rearrangement is a free mark if you use a fixed routine. You do not need to understand the whole paragraph. You only need to rule out three wrong strings. Use layers of elimination, and test only the part where the last two strings differ.

title: Layered elimination
text: Layered elimination Layer 1: the opener ban. Layer 2: the mandatory pair. Layer 3: the S6 check. Each layer is one question. Two layers usually finish the item. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Local-difference test
text: Local-difference test The two surviving strings differ in one place. Isolate that part and test only its two neighbours. Sentence Rearrangement

title: Odd-sentence radar
text: Odd-sentence radar For odd-one-out items, mark each sentence's key noun. Four share it. The odd one only orbits it. Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Spending 90 seconds building the full chain.
title.right: Two eliminations often finish the item. Stop when one string is left.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Refusing to mark an answer without full certainty.
title.right: Elimination already gives you the string. Mark it.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Reading the options before reading P, Q, R, S.
title.right: Read the parts first, then use the options to eliminate.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: In odd-one-out, choosing the least familiar sentence.
title.right: Choose the sentence that lacks the key noun.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Treating a dated sentence (*In August 2023...*) as the natural opener.
title.right: Check its anchors. It may end the story.

text: [object Object] Sentence Rearrangement

title.wrong: Linking two parts because they share a topic.
title.right: Trust grammar links: pronoun, *a* to *the*, *this + noun*, connector.

title: Spelling
text: Spelling · English Language · Choose the correctly spelt word · Find the wrongly spelt word · Misspelt word in a sentence · Plural and related forms · ie or ei · Doubling the last letter · Word endings (-ance / -ence, -able / -ible) · Silent letters and -cede / -ceed words

title: i before e — and the exceptions that fill the paper — Spelling
text: i before e — and the exceptions that fill the paper Long 'ee' with no c: ie Straight after c: ei ei exceptions with no c c + ie when c sounds 'sh' 'ay' or 'eye' sound: ei Longer word from a base word The old rhyme says: i before e, except after c . It works only when the pair makes the long 'ee' sound. Say the word first, then apply the rule. The paper also uses a short list of exceptions, such as weird , seize and foreign . Learn that list by heart.

title: The c-test
text: The c-test Is there a c right before the pair? Then choose ei (receive). No c? Usually choose ie (believe). Ten exceptions override this: weird, seize, height, foreign, sovereign, leisure, either, neither, their, protein. Spelling

title: Rhyme-anchor pairs
text: Rhyme-anchor pairs Some words match each other. Height and weight match. Believe and achieve match. Receive and deceive match. Fix one word of a pair and you get its partner free. Spelling

title: Say it in syllables
text: Say it in syllables Say the word slowly in your head: be-lieve, re-ceive. Your ear often confirms what your eye doubts. Spelling

title.wrong: Applying 'except after c' to words with no 'ee' sound, such as *neighbour*.
title.right: Say the word first. The c-rule works only for the long 'ee' sound.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *recieve* or *decieve*.
title.right: After c, the order is ei: receive, deceive, perceive, conceive.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *proficeint* or *sufficeint* because a c comes before the pair.
title.right: When c sounds 'sh', the spelling is -cient: proficient, sufficient, ancient.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *wierd*, *sieze* or *foriegn* by the ie habit.
title.right: These are exceptions with ei and no c: weird, seize, foreign.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *freind* or *mischeif*.
title.right: Friend and mischief keep ie. Remember fr-I-END.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Dropping the silent p in *receipt*, as in *receit*.
title.right: Receipt keeps its silent p.

title: Doubling consonants and one-letter betrayals — Spelling
text: Doubling consonants and one-letter betrayals Stressed final syllable: double Unstressed final syllable: no double Words with two sets of doubles Words with only one double British single l: travelled, cancelled Stress moves in the longer word A final consonant doubles before a vowel suffix only when the word ends in vowel + consonant and the stress is on the last syllable. So begin becomes beginning , but visit becomes visited . Some words also carry fixed double letters, such as accommodate and committee . Count those letters.

title: Stress decides doubling
text: Stress decides doubling Say the word. If the last syllable is stressed, double the consonant before a vowel suffix (begin, beginning; occur, occurred). If not, do not double (benefit, benefited). Spelling

title: Double-double checklist
text: Double-double checklist Five words need two sets of double letters: accommodate (c, m), committee (m, t), embarrass (r, s), occurrence (c, r), millennium (l, n). Count them. Spelling

title: Letter census
text: Letter census Count the repeated letters in each option. Accommodate must show two c's and two m's. Embarrass must show two r's and two s's. Cut any option that fails the count. Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *benefitted* or *targetted*.
title.right: The stress is early, so the t stays single: benefited, targeted.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *begining* or *refering*.
title.right: The last syllable is stressed, so the letter doubles: beginning, referring.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *accomodate* or *comittee* with one set of doubles.
title.right: Count both sets: accommodate has cc and mm. Committee has mm, tt and ee.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Doubling the wrong letter in *neccessary* or *reccomend*.
title.right: Necessary has one c and double s. Recommend has one c and double m.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *traveled* when the options are British.
title.right: British English doubles the l: travelled, cancelled, labelled.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *prefference* by copying *preferred*.
title.right: The stress moves in the longer word. Preference has one r after the f.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title: -able / -ible, -ance / -ence, -ant / -ent — Spelling
text: -able / -ible, -ance / -ence, -ant / -ent -ance or -ence -able or -ible Keep or drop the final e -ant or -ent adjective -cient family -y ending changes Three suffix pairs cause most ending mistakes: -able / -ible , -ance / -ence and -ant / -ent . No rule is perfect, but two tests work well. Ask if the stem is a complete word. Then think of the matching noun or adjective. Learn the word families in the tables as units.

title: Root trace
text: Root trace Strip the suffix and look at the root. Exist gives existence. Maintain gives maintenance. Resist gives resistance. Persist gives persistence. The root's own spelling helps decide the ending. Spelling

title: -fer means -ence
text: -fer means -ence Nouns from fer take -ence: reference, preference, difference, inference. The verb doubles by stress: refer, referring. Spelling

title: The -cient family
text: The -cient family Sufficient, efficient and ancient all end in -cient. Science is sci + ence, and conscience is con + science. Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *independant* or *persistant* by sound.
title.right: Match the adjective: independent, persistent, dependent.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *resistence* or *maintainance*.
title.right: Resistance takes -ance. The noun from maintain is maintenance.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *noticable* or *changable*.
title.right: Keep the e after a soft c or g: noticeable, changeable.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *responsable* or *indispensible*.
title.right: Use the whole-word test: responsible has a non-word stem, so -ible. Indispensable has a whole-word stem, so -able.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *sufficent* or *efficiant*.
title.right: These end in -cient: sufficient, efficient, ancient.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *arguement* or *truely*.
title.right: Argue and true lose the e: argument, truly.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title: The trap-word bank: silent letters and inherited mistakes — Spelling
text: The trap-word bank: silent letters and inherited mistakes Silent letter -ceed, -cede or -sede Root letter changed in the longer word Borrowed word Missing letter: the root drops a letter Root letter survives: govern-ment Some words are spelt wrongly again and again, so setters choose them. Each one hides a silent letter, a missing letter or a borrowed pattern. Learn the bank in small groups, and give each word a hook.

title: The n-test for -ment words
text: The n-test for -ment words Government is govern + ment. Environment is environ + ment. The root's final n must survive. Ask what the root is, and the letter reappears. Spelling

title: Three -ceed, one -sede
text: Three -ceed, one -sede Proceed, succeed and exceed are the only -ceed words. Supersede is the only -sede word. Every other word with this sound ends in -cede. Spelling

title: Plurals already plural
text: Plurals already plural Criteria, phenomena and stimuli are already plurals. An option that adds -s to them (criterias) is wrong. Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *priviledge* or *goverment* by sound.
title.right: Use the hook: privilege has no d. Government keeps the n of govern.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *seperate* or *definate*.
title.right: Separate has 'a rat' in it. Definite ends in -inite.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Writing *preceed* or *procede*.
title.right: Only proceed, succeed and exceed end in -ceed. Precede ends in -cede.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Keeping the root unchanged: *pronounciation*, *nineth*.
title.right: The root changes: pronunciation, ninth.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Dropping the silent letter: *Wensday*, *dout*.
title.right: Say the word as it is spelt: Wednesday, doubt.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Swapping letters in a borrowed word: *entreprenuer*.
title.right: Split it into parts: entre + pre + neur.

title: Exam strategy: how to judge a spelling you have never seen — Spelling
text: Exam strategy: how to judge a spelling you have never seen Choose the correct spelling Find the misspelt word (four different words) Misspelt word inside a sentence Classical plural Long word: check syllable by syllable Prefix + root: both letters stay Spelling questions come in a few shapes. Some show four versions of one word. Some show four different words and ask for the wrong one. In both, you find the spot that differs or fails, and you apply one test. A short daily routine turns recognising words into spelling them.

title: Difference-first reading
text: Difference-first reading Do not read four full words. Find the one position where they differ. That spot is the whole question. Spelling

title: Syllable count
text: Syllable count Count the syllables. Mischievous has three. Rhythm has two. A wrong spelling often forces a syllable that cannot be said. Spelling

title: Write-from-memory drill
text: Write-from-memory drill Seeing a word is not the same as spelling it. Cover the list, write the words, mark the misses and repeat tomorrow. The misses shrink each round. Spelling

title.wrong: Reading all four options in full.
title.right: Find the one spot where they differ and check only that.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Adding -s to a classical plural: *criterias*, *crisises*.
title.right: Use the classical plural: criteria, crises.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Checking meaning in a misspelt-word-in-a-sentence item.
title.right: Ignore the sentence and check each word on its own.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Marking British forms like *recognised* as wrong.
title.right: British forms are correct in these exams.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Choosing the option that merely looks familiar.
title.right: Choose the one that follows a rule: sound, stress or whole-word.

text: [object Object] Spelling

title.wrong: Leaving a spelling item blank.
title.right: Make one informed choice. There is no reason to skip it.

title: Synonyms & Antonyms
text: Synonyms & Antonyms · English Language · Synonym (nearest in meaning) · Antonym (opposite in meaning) · Guess a hard word from its parts · Opposite that is not made by a prefix · Word inside a sentence · Near answers with different strength · Vocabulary in fill-in questions · Synonym and antonym mixed

title: The root-word method: decode words you have never seen — Synonyms & Antonyms
text: The root-word method: decode words you have never seen Prefix gives the direction Root gives the core meaning Chunk a long word False-root trap word Root family across two words Most hard English words are built from small parts: a prefix, a root and a suffix. If you know about 40 of these parts, you can work out the meaning of words you have never seen. Use this method to guess an unknown word in a synonym or antonym question.

title: Split, then eliminate
text: Split, then eliminate Cut the unknown word at its joins, translate the parts you know, and remove options that clash. One sure root can remove two options. Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Learn roots as families
text: Learn roots as families Learn words in root groups, not in alphabet order. The dict family: dictate, verdict, predict, contradict. The loqu family: eloquent, loquacious, soliloquy. Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Warm or cold
text: Warm or cold Roots carry a feeling. Bene-, eu- and am- are warm. Mal-, dys-, phob- and mis- are cold. When stuck, pick an option with the same feeling. Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Skipping the prefix and guessing from the root alone.
title.right: Read the prefix first. It tells you the direction of the meaning.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Trusting a root when you already know the word.
title.right: Your memory of the word beats the root. Roots are for unknown words.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Picking energise for ENERVATE because it looks like energy.
title.right: Learn the five fixed words: enervate, restive, inflammable, invaluable, noisome.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Ignoring the word class.
title.right: Check -ous, -tion, -ise endings. Remove options of a different class.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Learning roots as a list only.
title.right: Attach each root to two real words. Use the words to recall the root.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Choosing the nearest meaning: elimination by class, degree, charge — Synonyms & Antonyms
text: Choosing the nearest meaning: elimination by class, degree, charge Word-class filter Strength match Tone match Meaning from the sentence Overlap, not association A synonym question asks for the word closest in meaning. You do not need the exact dictionary meaning. You only need to remove three options that fail one of four filters: word class, idea class, strength and tone.

title: The replace test
text: The replace test The right synonym can replace the word in most sentences. If the sentence changes meaning, the option is only related. Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Tone sorts half the options
text: Tone sorts half the options Mark the given word + or - (notorious is -, celebrated is +). Options with the other mark can go without more thought. Synonyms & Antonyms

title: The strength ruler
text: The strength ruler Draw a line from mild to extreme. Put the word and the two surviving options on it. The option at the same mark wins. Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Choosing an option because it is related to the word.
title.right: Choose the option that can replace the word in a sentence.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Picking a noun for a verb because it looks close.
title.right: Check the word class before the meaning.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Taking a mild word for an extreme one (big for ENORMOUS).
title.right: Match strength. An extreme word needs an extreme answer.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Ignoring the tone (celebrated for NOTORIOUS).
title.right: Mark the word + or - first. Keep only options with the same mark.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Answering from the most common meaning when a sentence is given.
title.right: Read the sentence and answer for the meaning used there.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Antonyms: prefix flips and real opposites — Synonyms & Antonyms
text: Antonyms: prefix flips and real opposites Opposite on the same scale Prefix-flip false opposite Strike the synonyms first Same word class Direction or role pair An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning. The right option reverses the idea. It does not just differ, and it does not just remove the idea. Beware of words that look like opposites because of a prefix but really mean the same.

title: Pair-of-sentences test
text: Pair-of-sentences test Put the word and each option in the same short sentence. The option that gives a real contradiction is the antonym. Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Guess the flip first
text: Guess the flip first Before reading the options, guess the opposite yourself (conformity, then nonconformity). If your guess is in the options, mark it. Synonyms & Antonyms

title: Absence is not opposition
text: Absence is not opposition Cross out options that only lack the quality. Careful does not fight brave. Cowardly does. Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Choosing a word that only differs (careful for BRAVE).
title.right: Pick the word at the other end of the scale (cowardly).

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Building the opposite by adding a prefix (valuable for INVALUABLE).
title.right: Learn the true meaning first. Invaluable means very valuable.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Choosing a synonym because it 'feels close'.
title.right: Strike every synonym at once. They are decoys.

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Taking absence as opposition (ignore for PRAISE).
title.right: The opposite must reverse the idea (criticise).

text: [object Object] Synonyms & Antonyms

title.wrong: Choosing a noun for an adjective (opacity for TRANSPARENT).
title.right: Match the word class. The answer is opaque.

An indirect tax is passed on to buyers, like GST. GST began on 1 July 2017, and GST 2.0 cut it to two main slabs, 5% and 18%, from 22 September 2025. The new Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026.

You find that rule and apply it to the third number. Most rules are simple: multiply and add, square or cube, or work on the digits. Always check the rule on the model pair before you use it.

title: Multiply-and-add rule
text: Multiply-and-add rule a is the first number, b the second. Find k and r from the model pair, then check. b = k a + r Analogy

title: Square family
text: Square family Try these when b is close to the square of a. b = a^2 r,\ a(a+1),\ (a+1)^2 Analogy

title: Digit rules
text: Digit rules Not allowed when the whole-number note is given. b = ,\ ,\ ( )^2 Analogy

title: The size test picks the family
text: The size test picks the family Compare b with a before anything else. A few times a: multiply and add. Near a squared: square family. Very large: cubes. Smaller: roots or digit rules. Analogy

title: Check the rule on the model pair
text: Check the rule on the model pair Whatever rule you guess, make sure it gives b from a exactly. The check takes two seconds and prevents most wrong answers. Analogy

title.wrong: Using a rule that nearly fits (12 : 49 read as 12 × 4).
title.right: The rule must give the exact number: 12 × 4 + 1 = 49.

title.right: Use exactly the same rule on both pairs.

title.right: With that note, use only operations on the full number.

title.wrong: Forcing a rule when the answer is not in the options.
title.right: If your answer is missing, try the next family in the size table.

title.wrong: Missing a simple reversal: 27 : 72 read as × 2 + 18.
title.right: If the digits are just swapped, the rule is reversal. Prefer the simpler rule.

title: Number sets (triads) analogy — Analogy
text: Number sets (triads) analogy Chain sets (the same step twice) Third number from the first two Power sets (a, a², a³ and near-powers) Middle number links the outer two Third number from the difference You are shown two or more sets of three numbers, such as (6, 13, 27) and (8, 17, 35). One hidden rule links the numbers inside every set. Find that rule, check it on every set, then pick the option set that follows it. Most papers say to use whole numbers only, so digit tricks are not allowed.

title: Chain rule
text: Chain rule a, b, c are the three numbers of a set. One step is used twice. b = ka + r, c = kb + r Analogy

title: Third from first two
text: Third from first two Test on every model set. c = ab,\ a^2 + b^2,\ k(a+b),\ k(a-b) Analogy

title: Power set
text: Power set Near-squares and near-cubes of the first number. (a,\ a^2 r,\ a^3 r) Analogy

title: Compute only the last number
text: Compute only the last number Once you have the rule, work out what the last number of each option should be. Traps nearly always change only that number, so one pass finds the answer. Analogy

title.wrong: Breaking numbers into digits when the whole-number note is given.
title.right: Use only operations on full numbers: +, −, ×, ÷, squares, cubes.

title.wrong: Accepting a rule that fits the first model set but not the second.
title.right: Check the rule on every model set before looking at the options.

text: [object Object] Analogy

title.wrong: Checking only the first two numbers of an option.
title.right: Compute the third number too. Traps are usually off by 1 to 3 there.

title.wrong: Trying only chains and giving up.
title.right: Go through the four families in order: chain, third from two, powers, middle link.

text: Two columns: letters and numbers Make one column for the letters and one for the numbers. Solve each column on its own. An error then stays inside one column. Analogy

title: How to solve blood-relation questions — Blood Relations
text: How to solve blood-relation questions Which direction is the question asking Gender never fixed: cannot be determined Two sentences, one small tree Counting members of a family Mother's side and father's side A blood-relation question gives you a few sentences about one family. Your job is to draw them as a family tree and read the answer off it. Two habits protect every mark: never guess a gender, and answer in the direction the question asks. The method below works for every question in this topic.

title: Mirror pairs
text: Mirror pairs Every relation has a mirror. If A is B's uncle, B is A's nephew or niece. ,\ Blood Relations

title: Marriage words
text: Marriage words Spouse's parent = father/mother-in-law. Sibling's spouse or spouse's sibling = brother/sister-in-law. Blood Relations

title: Cousin
text: Cousin An uncle's or aunt's child is always a cousin, never a nephew. = Blood Relations

title: Write each sentence as an arrow
text: Write each sentence as an arrow In the margin, turn every sentence into an arrow: 'Suresh's daughter is Pooja' becomes Suresh to Pooja (F). When every sentence is an arrow, the tree draws itself. Blood Relations

title: Flip the word, not the tree
text: Flip the word, not the tree One tree answers both directions. Keep the drawing, swap to the mirror word: father goes to son, uncle to nephew, grandfather to grandson. Blood Relations

title.wrong: Giving a gender no word stated, like calling every cousin 'he'.
title.right: Mark M or F only from gendered words. Leave the rest blank and let the blank decide the option.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Answering the reverse direction: 'grandfather' when asked how the elder relates to the child.
title.right: Start from the person named after 'related to'. Then walk to the other person.

title.wrong: Calling an uncle's child a nephew.
title.right: Uncle's or aunt's child is a cousin. Nephew is a sibling's child.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Reading 'only son' as 'only child'.
title.right: 'Only son' leaves room for sisters. 'Only child' leaves no sibling at all.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Putting a married couple on different rows.
title.right: A couple always shares one row, one generation.
