title: Multi-statement tree puzzles — Blood Relations
text: Multi-statement tree puzzles Chains across generations Marriage links: the in-law words Counting males and females in a family Shuffled sentences, one tree Cousins across two branches These questions give three to six sentences about one family, in a shuffled order, and then ask a relation. Do not read them in order. Find the oldest person, put them on top, and hang everyone else below. A tree built top-down never needs redoing.

title: Start from the root
text: Start from the root The root is the person nobody calls a child. Build downward from there. Every statement then clicks into an empty slot. Blood Relations

title: Count arrows, then gender
text: Count arrows, then gender The arrow count picks the family of the word (father, grandfather, great-grandfather). Only then does gender pick inside it. Never guess the word first and draw later. Blood Relations

title.wrong: Reading the sentences in exam order and answering from memory.
title.right: Find the root, build top-down, then answer from the tree.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Calling an uncle's or aunt's child a nephew or niece.
title.right: That child is a cousin. A nephew is a sibling's child.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Leaving a spouse out of a count of family members.
title.right: Everyone named, married-in or born-in, gets one box in the tree.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Counting a person whose gender was never fixed.
title.right: Leave blank-gender names out of male and female counts.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Mixing up the two ends of an in-law word.
title.right: Child's spouse is son or daughter-in-law. Spouse's parent is father or mother-in-law.

title: Pointing and introducing — Blood Relations
text: Pointing and introducing Long phrase, decoded layer by layer The phrase returns to the speaker Two readings fit: cannot be determined The reverse ask 'Pointing to a man, Rita said: he is the only son of my mother's mother's only child.' The whole family hides inside one spoken phrase, and the speaker is part of it. Peel the phrase from the inside out, one link per line. Watch for phrases that fold back on the speaker, like 'my mother's only child

title: One layer per line
text: One layer per line Underline the innermost 'my' and work outward. Each line of rough work resolves one 'of'. Then place the speaker and the target in a two-person sketch. Blood Relations

title: Scan for the fold-back
text: Scan for the fold-back Before peeling anything, scan the phrase for 'my mother's only child', 'my father's only son', 'my mother's only daughter'. If one is there, test the speaker's gender against it first. Blood Relations

title.wrong: Reading 'only son' as 'only child'.
title.right: 'Only son' bars other boys only. Sisters may exist.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Forgetting the speaker is a person in the tree.
title.right: Every 'my' belongs to the speaker. Test fold-back phrases first.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Answering in the reverse direction: 'his sister' instead of 'her brother'.
title.right: Check which person the question names after 'related to'.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Peeling a three-layer phrase in one jump.
title.right: One layer per line. Slow rough work is fast here.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Choosing a relation when two families both fit the phrase.
title.right: Build both readings. If both fit, answer 'Cannot be determined'.

title: Coded (symbol) relations — Blood Relations
text: Coded (symbol) relations Two symbols, three letters Three symbols, four letters Reverse ask on a coded string Build the string for a given relation The exam invents private symbols: 'P + Q means P is the father of Q'. Then a string like A + B x C hides a small family. Decode one symbol at a time into a plain sentence. Each symbol fixes the gender of its first letter only. Draw the tree, then answer in the question's direction.

title: Write the sentences under the string
text: Write the sentences under the string For each symbol, write its one-line sentence under the string, then draw. Six symbols become three short sentences, and the drawing finishes the job. Blood Relations

title: Audit genders before answering
text: Audit genders before answering Before marking, list every letter with the gender its symbols fixed. If the asked word needs a gender that stayed blank, the answer is the neutral word or 'Cannot be determined'. Blood Relations

title.wrong: Decoding a whole string in one breath.
title.right: Cut at every symbol. One sentence per cut, then draw.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Fixing the gender of the second letter from the symbol.
title.right: 'A is the brother of B' fixes A only. B stays blank until another symbol fixes it.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Answering the string's direction instead of the question's.
title.right: Read the question. If it asks the reverse pair, give the mirror word.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Forgetting the spouse of a parent is also a parent.
title.right: If B is C's wife and B is A's parent, then C is A's parent too.

text: [object Object] Blood Relations

title.wrong: Marking 'Cannot be determined' without checking every symbol.
title.right: List the gender marks first. Only a truly blank needed gender allows that answer.

title: Classification (Odd One Out)
text: Classification (Odd One Out) · Reasoning · Find the odd one out · Odd one out with a second check · Animals and plants · Same use or job · Prime and non-prime numbers · Squares and cubes · Letter groups with a step · Word pairs with a different link · Pairs with one wrong fact · Number sets with the same steps

title: The idea of odd one out — Classification (Odd One Out)
text: The idea of odd one out Standard odd one out (three alike, one different) Select the item that belongs to the same group Two-level (tie-break) odd one out Word-structure (spelling) odd one out Five options: four alike, one different Classification means putting things into groups. The exam shows four (sometimes five) similar items. Three of them share one hidden feature and one does not. Your whole job is to state the rule the majority follows, then pick the item that breaks it. Test checkable rules first: numbers, letter steps

title: Write the majority rule, not the exception
text: Write the majority rule, not the exception Instead of hunting the odd item, write the rule the other three follow. Confirm each of the three obeys it and the last one breaks it. This stops you marking an item that is merely unusual. Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: Stopping at the first difference you notice.
title.right: Test the rule on all items. It must separate exactly one from the rest.

text: [object Object] Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: Assuming the odd item sits at the last position.
title.right: The setter shuffles positions. Check every option.

text: [object Object] Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: Using a loose category ("all are animals") where a tighter one exists ("all are birds").
title.right: Prefer the tightest rule that still groups the majority.

text: [object Object] Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: In "which belongs to the group" questions, marking the item that is different.
title.right: There the answer is the one that FITS the group of three.

text: [object Object] Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: Needing a rare fact to justify an answer.
title.right: The exam uses school-level facts only. A rare fact means the rule is wrong.

title: Word odd one out — Classification (Odd One Out)
text: Word odd one out Category break (animals, plants, living things) Function / use break Property break (state, material, natural/man-made) GK set (capitals, instruments, units) Meaning group (three synonyms, one antonym) Four words come from overlapping fields. Three share a category, a use or a property, and one breaks it. The exam recycles the same pools: animals, computer parts, metals, instruments, state capitals. Say the group of the majority in one sentence. If all four fit, switch to a property level: input o

title: Category first, then a binary property
text: Category first, then a binary property First find the broad category shared by three words. If the fourth also fits that category, switch to a binary property: salt or fresh, input or output, element or alloy, male or female. One word will stand alone on the other side. Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: Choosing by rarity ("turtle is uncommon").
title.right: Choose by a structural difference: shell, scales, habitat, class.

text: [object Object] Classification (Odd One Out)

title.wrong: Missing the input-versus-output split in device questions.
title.right: For computer parts, always ask: does it send data in or bring it out?

text: Number odd one out Prime vs composite Perfect square / perfect cube Multiples / divisibility Digit sum / digit product Two-level: same power, odd or even root Number forms (n²+1, n³−1, n(n+1)) Four numbers are given. Three share a number property and one breaks it. You do not need long calculation; you need a fixed list of properties to test in order. The list: prime or composite, perfect square or cube, multiples, digit rules, odd or even, and near-forms like a square plus one. When the

title: Divisibility by 11
text: Divisibility by 11 S = sums of alternate digits from the left; e.g. 2728: (2+2) − (7+8) = −11, divisible. |S_{odd} - S_{even}| 0 Classification (Odd One Out)

title: Perfect square endings
text: Perfect square endings A square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8 — instant elimination. n^2 \{0,1,4,5,6,9\} Classification (Odd One Out)

title: Digit sum rule for 9
text: Digit sum rule for 9 S(n) is the sum of the digits of n. 9 n S(n) 0 9 Classification (Odd One Out)

title: Last-digit scan for squares
text: Last-digit scan for squares Squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. An option ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 cannot be a square. For the rest, place the number between two known squares. Classification (Odd One Out)

title: Prime check by small divisors
text: Prime check by small divisors To test a number under 200 for prime, divide only by 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13. Memorise the fake-prime list: 51, 57, 87, 91, 119, 133, 143, 161. Classification (Odd One Out)

title.right: 1 is neither prime nor composite. 2 is the only even prime.

The step tuple turns a feel question into simple arithmetic. If the tuples match

title: Step of a cluster
text: Step of a cluster Q is the alphabet position. Compute steps for every option; three must match as tuples. s_i = Q(L_{i+1}) - Q(L_i) Classification (Odd One Out)

title: Opposite-pair sum
text: Opposite-pair sum Letter pairs whose positions add to 27: AZ, BY, ..., MN. Q(X) + Q(Y) = 27 Classification (Odd One Out)

title: Step tuples in one line
text: Step tuples in one line Under each cluster write its steps: ACE → (+2, +2), BDF → (+2, +2), GIK → (+2, +2), MOP → (+2, +1). The mismatched tuple is the answer. No vowel counting is needed. Classification (Odd One Out)

text: Vowel count as tiebreaker If the step tuples agree, or the clusters look irregular, count the vowels (A, E, I, O, U). Three clusters with no vowel and one with a vowel (or the reverse) is a complete exam pattern. Classification (Odd One Out)

title: How every series is cracked — Series (Number & Letter)
text: How every series is cracked Find the next term with the difference ladder A missing term in the middle Fractions, decimals or halving Two missing terms: pick the right pair Find the first term A series is a list of numbers written in a fixed order. Every term comes from the one before it by one small rule. Your job is to name that rule, then find the next term or the missing term. The difference ladder finds the rule in most questions: subtract neighbours, and subtract again if needed

title: Gap between terms
text: Gap between terms Write these gaps under the series. If they are not clear, take gaps of the gaps. d_n = a_{n+1} - a_n Series (Number & Letter)

title: Same number added
text: Same number added d is the equal gap. Use it when the first row of gaps is constant. a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d Series (Number & Letter)

title: Two rows of gaps in ten seconds
text: Two rows of gaps in ten seconds Write the gaps under the series. If they are not equal, write the gaps of the gaps. Stop when a row is clear. Then work back up. Series (Number & Letter)

title: Say the rule aloud in words
text: Say the rule aloud in words Before you calculate, say the rule in one plain sentence, like 'add 3, then add 6, then add 9'. If you cannot say it in a sentence, the rule is wrong. Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Guessing the rule from the last two terms only.
title.right: The rule must fit every term. Test it from the first term.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Stopping after one row of gaps when it is not equal.
title.right: Take gaps of the gaps. The second row often shows the rule.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Filling a middle blank without checking the next term.
title.right: Check that the term after the blank comes from your answer.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Reading decimals or fractions as unusual rules.
title.right: Use the same ideas. Decimals follow ×k or ÷k. Fractions split into tops and bottoms.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Trying squares first on every series.
title.right: Look at the size first. Slow growth means gaps. Fast growth means ratio.

title: Number series — Series (Number & Letter)
text: Number series Same or growing gap Multiply, then add or subtract Squares, cubes and n × (n + 1) Gaps of gaps Two series mixed together Mixed steps: ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2 and so on Sum of the earlier terms Gaps that are squares, cubes, primes or powers of 2 Most number-series questions come from eight families. Learn the families, and each question becomes a quick check against a short list. Slow growth points to gaps. Fast growth points to multiplying. Going up and down points to two series mixed together.

title: Same gap (AP)
text: Same gap (AP) d is the equal gap from the ladder. a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d Series (Number & Letter)

title: Multiply then adjust
text: Multiply then adjust Try k = 2 and 3 first, with r = 1 or 2. a_{n+1} = k a_n r Series (Number & Letter)

title: Squares family
text: Squares family If the second gaps are all 2, the series is built on n squared. a_n = n^2 k \ \ n^2 + n Series (Number & Letter)

title: Same ratio (GP)
text: Same ratio (GP) r is the fixed ratio. Test ×2, ×3 and ×1.5. a_n = a_1 r^{\,n-1} Series (Number & Letter)

title: Ratio test before anything fancy
text: Ratio test before anything fancy Divide each term by the one before it. If the result is close to 2 or 3, try ×k ± r. Find r from what is left over. Series (Number & Letter)

title: Split a jumpy series
text: Split a jumpy series If the terms go up and down, write the odd places on one line and the even places on another. Solve each line on its own. Then find which line the asked place belongs to. Series (Number & Letter)

title: Cubes hiding in the gaps
text: Cubes hiding in the gaps If the gaps grow very fast, check for cubes (1, 8, 27, 64, 125) or powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16). Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Trying only 'add' on a series that grows fast.
title.right: Look at the size first. Fast growth needs a ratio test.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Stopping at the first row of gaps.
title.right: Take the gaps of the gaps. Look for squares, cubes and powers of 2.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Reading an up-and-down series as one series.
title.right: Split into odd and even places. Then find the place asked.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Using the last two terms to guess the rule.
title.right: Test the rule on every term from the start.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Forgetting that ×k ± r needs a small leftover.
title.right: After ×2 or ×3, find what is left over. That is the r.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Giving the second-gap answer as the next term.
title.right: Climb back up: next second gap, then next gap, then next term.

title: Letter series — Series (Number & Letter)
text: Letter series Single letters with a constant step Rising or falling step between letters Two letter series mixed together Letter-cluster series Positions that are squares or primes A missing letter in the middle Clusters that cross Z Every letter series is a number series in disguise. Give each letter its place in the alphabet, then solve it as a number series. Go back to letters at the end, and wrap around after Z.

title: Opposite letter
text: Opposite letter A and Z, B and Y, and so on. Each pair adds up to 27. = 27 - Series (Number & Letter)

title: Wrap around
text: Wrap around Use this whenever the rule takes you past Z or before A. > 26 - 26,\ \ < 1 + 26 Series (Number & Letter)

title: A step row under the letters
text: A step row under the letters Write the place under every letter, then the gap between places. Work on the numbers only. Convert to a letter once, at the end. Series (Number & Letter)

title: Wrap around with the number 26
text: Wrap around with the number 26 Never count letters on your fingers past Z. Add or subtract 26 on the number, then convert. Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Counting on your fingers from A each time.
title.right: Use the anchors E, J, O, T, Y and count one or two steps from the nearest.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Forgetting to wrap around after Z.
title.right: If the place is above 26, subtract 26 before you convert to a letter.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Solving a cluster as one long series.
title.right: Solve each letter slot as its own series.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Reading a jumpy series as one series.
title.right: Split it into odd and even places, or check for steps that take turns.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Mixing up forward places and reverse places.
title.right: A = 1 counting forward. Z = 1 counting backward. Reverse place = 27 − place.

title: Alphanumeric series — Series (Number & Letter)
text: Alphanumeric series Letter and number as two independent tracks Number equals the place of the letter Terms with two letters and a number A missing term in the middle Number equals the place squared Number comes first An alphanumeric term mixes a letter and a number, like A3 or D6. Most of the time the letters follow one series and the numbers follow another. Solve the two tracks separately, then join the answers in the same format as the terms.

title: Two columns, two answers, one join
text: Two columns, two answers, one join Write letters in one column and numbers in the other. Solve each column on its own. Join only at the end, in the format of the question. Series (Number & Letter)

title: Test the letter-place link first
text: Test the letter-place link first Check whether the number equals the place of the letter, or its square. If yes, you only need the next letter. Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Picking an option with the right letter but a number from a wrong rule.
title.right: Solve the number track on its own. Then match both parts.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Writing the answer in the wrong order, like 32J for J32.
title.right: Copy the format of the given terms.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Using the letter's step for the number, or the number's step for the letter.
title.right: Keep two separate columns. Each has its own step.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Not checking whether the number is the place of the letter.
title.right: Test this link first. It is a common rule.

title: Wrong number in the series — Series (Number & Letter)
text: Wrong number in the series Wrong term in an equal-gap or growing-gap series Wrong term in a ratio or multiply-and-add series Wrong term in a squares or cubes series Wrong term in an alternate series Wrong term in a letter series Wrong term in a gaps-of-gaps series The first term is wrong In a wrong-number question the series is already complete, but one term does not fit. You must name that term as it is shown, not the correct value. The wrong term sits between two gaps that look wrong.

title: Ladder with one broken rung
text: Ladder with one broken rung Write the gaps. Find two bad gaps side by side. The term between them is the wrong term. Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Giving the correct value as the answer.
title.right: The answer is the wrong term as it is shown in the question.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Blaming the term after the first bad gap.
title.right: The wrong term sits between two bad gaps.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Testing the rule only on the last few terms.
title.right: Test it from the first term. The first term can also be wrong.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Using the wrong term to build the next term.
title.right: Rebuild each term from the correct one, starting from the beginning.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Missing an alternate series.
title.right: If the gaps zigzag, split into odd and even places.

title: Repeating letter series — fill the blanks — Series (Number & Letter)
text: Repeating letter series — fill the blanks Fixed repeating block Growing block Mirror block Rotating block Block with a repeated letter Up-and-down walk A line of small letters has blanks, like a _ c a b _ a b c _ b c. The line follows one repeating pattern. Find the pattern, fill the blanks from left to right, and match the option. The pattern is a fixed block, a growing block, a mirror block or a rotating block.

title: Write the blocks one below another
text: Write the blocks one below another Cut the line into equal rows. Each column must hold one letter. Blanks take the letter of their column. Series (Number & Letter)

title: A double letter marks a mirror turn
text: A double letter marks a mirror turn If the line has a doubled letter like rr or nn, the block probably reads forward and then backward. The block is twice the length of the first half. Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Guessing the block size without counting the places.
title.right: Count all places first. The block size divides the total (or the parts add up to it).

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Filling the blanks from right to left.
title.right: Fill from left to right. The options are written in that order.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Not reading the full line after filling.
title.right: Read the whole line once. One wrong letter breaks the repeat.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Treating a growing block as a fixed block.
title.right: If the parts get longer, split the line as 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 places.

text: [object Object] Series (Number & Letter)

title.wrong: Swapping letters in a block with a repeated letter.
title.right: Fill column by column, not from memory.

title: Statement & Conclusion
text: Statement & Conclusion · Reasoning · Two conclusions after a statement · Statement with numbers · "Only those who ..." trap · Three conclusions · Statement and assumption · Assumption in a decision · Course of action · Relief and prevention

title: Statement and conclusions — Statement & Conclusion
text: Statement and conclusions Extreme word, over-general claim or outside cause Data-based conclusion The only-rule applied to a person Restatement and clear implication Percentage change and comparison A future guess The every-rule and the wrong direction Soft words against hard words You get a short statement and some conclusions. A conclusion follows only if the statement alone forces it. Real-life truth does not matter. Use only the statement as evidence.

title: The extreme-word filter
text: The extreme-word filter Circle words like only, all, always, never, surely, best, entire and must. If the conclusion has one and the statement does not, it almost always fails. Statement & Conclusion

title: Needed is not the same as enough
text: Needed is not the same as enough 'Only X can do Y' means X is required. It does not mean X is enough. Check which way the conclusion runs. Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Judging the conclusion by what is true in real life.
title.right: Judge it only by the statement. Real-life facts are not evidence.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting a conclusion because it sounds sensible.
title.right: Ask if the statement forces it. Sensible is not enough.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Reading 'only X can' as 'every X will'.
title.right: Only-X tells you who is out. It does not tell you who is in.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Reading an average as a limit or as each value.
title.right: An average gives a total. It does not give the maximum or each value.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Treating sales as profit.
title.right: Profit needs the cost. If the cost is not given, profit is unknown.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Rejecting a soft word like 'some' or 'likely'.
title.right: Soft words are safe when the reading is fair.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title: Statement and assumptions — Statement & Conclusion
text: Statement and assumptions Advice or request: the negation test Advertisement or notice Total-effect or extreme assumption Decision or policy: possible and purposeful Appeal or request Comparison with rivals An assumption that makes the statement unnecessary An assumption is an idea the speaker takes for granted before speaking. It is not written in the statement. Without it, the statement would make no sense. The negation test finds it.

title: The negation test
text: The negation test Put 'not' into the assumption. Does the speaker still have a reason to speak? If not, the assumption is implicit. Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Confusing an assumption with a conclusion.
title.right: An assumption is what the speaker believes before speaking. A conclusion follows after.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting a total effect such as 'all accidents will stop'.
title.right: The speaker needs only some good effect. A total result is not implicit.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting a comparison with rivals in an advert.
title.right: An advert need not claim to be the best. It only needs some buyers.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting a strong assumption because it sounds true.
title.right: Use the negation test. If the statement still makes sense, it is not implicit.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting something that makes the statement pointless.
title.right: If the assumption would make the statement unnecessary, it is not implicit.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title: Courses of action — Statement & Conclusion
text: Courses of action A practical fix against a blanket ban Short-term relief plus long-term fix An unrelated step Punishing all against acting on those responsible Inquiry before action when the cause is unknown Permanent shutdown for a local problem Awareness, repair and regulation together The statement describes a problem. A course of action is a step to deal with it. A step follows if it is practical, proportionate and related to the problem, and the right authority can take it.

title: The proportion check
text: The proportion check Ask: would a sensible official do this tomorrow? Inspecting, repairing, warning, supplying and treating usually pass. Banning, shutting forever and blaming everyone usually fail. Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Picking a strong step because it sounds firm.
title.right: Pick the step that is practical and in proportion.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Rejecting a relief step because it is not permanent.
title.right: Relief and a long-term fix can both follow.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting a step that punishes everyone.
title.right: Act against those responsible. Do not punish the innocent.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Accepting a step unrelated to the problem.
title.right: Check that the step touches the stated problem.

text: [object Object] Statement & Conclusion

title.wrong: Punishing a person before an inquiry when the cause is unknown.
title.right: Order an inquiry first. Then act against those found responsible.

title: Syllogism
text: Syllogism · Reasoning · Two statements, two conclusions · Three statements in a chain · "Is a possibility" conclusion · Either-or conclusions · "Only a few" statements · Turn a statement around · Try to break the conclusion · Possibility blocked by a "No"

title: What a syllogism is and how to test it — Syllogism
text: What a syllogism is and how to test it Some + All chain (shared member travels) All-chain with a conversion conclusion No + Some gives Some-not Conversion-only pair Three-statement chain Some-not does not travel Two Some statements A syllogism gives two or three statements that you must accept as true. Then you judge conclusions. A conclusion follows only if it holds in every picture that fits the statements. Real-world facts do not matter. Try to break each conclusion with one picture.

title: Transitivity of All
text: Transitivity of All 'All A are B + All B are C → All A are C' is the only freely chained rule. A B B C A C Syllogism

title: Conversion of All
text: Conversion of All Valid (classes are assumed non-empty): 'Some B are A' follows. A B B A Syllogism

title: Conversion of No / Some
text: Conversion of No / Some Both convert symmetrically. A B B A; A B B A Syllogism

title: Find the shared term
text: Find the shared term The conclusion must join the two outer terms. Find the term that appears in both statements, and ask what travels through it. Syllogism

title: One counter-picture kills it
text: One counter-picture kills it You do not need to prove a conclusion. You need only one picture that fits the statements and breaks it. Syllogism

title.wrong: Rejecting a statement because it is false in real life.
title.right: Accept every statement as true. Reason only from the statements.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Reading 'All A are B' as 'All B are A'.
title.right: All does not reverse. Only 'Some B are A' follows.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Joining two 'Some' statements into a conclusion.
title.right: Two 'Some' statements never join. Draw the overlaps apart to test.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Passing a 'Some-not' through an All.
title.right: The A outside B may or may not be a C. Nothing follows.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Drawing the picture that supports the conclusion.
title.right: Draw the smallest picture that fits the statements. Then try to break the conclusion.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title: Possibility conclusions — Syllogism
text: Possibility conclusions Plain possibility (nothing blocks it) Possibility blocked by a No statement Possibility with only-a-few statements Possibility paired with a definite conclusion Possibility that empties a group A possibility conclusion asks a lighter question: can this be true without breaking a statement? One supporting picture is enough to make it follow. It fails only when a statement makes it impossible.

title: Defence lawyer thinking
text: Defence lawyer thinking For a possibility, flip your mindset. Build one picture where it holds. Done. Syllogism

title.wrong: Looking for a picture where the possibility must hold.
title.right: You need only one picture where it can hold.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Ignoring the 'No' statement when you draw the possibility.
title.right: A 'No' statement blocks every picture that puts a member across it.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Saying 'No B are A' is possible after 'All A are B'.
title.right: Groups are non-empty. A member of A is a member of B, so B and A must meet.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Saying 'All A are B' is possible after 'Only a few A are B'.
title.right: Only a few guarantees an A outside B, so that possibility is dead.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Judging a definite conclusion by the one-picture rule.
title.right: A definite conclusion must hold in every picture.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title: Either-or (complementary pairs) — Syllogism
text: Either-or (complementary pairs) (All, Some-not) complementary pair (Some, No) complementary pair Fake complementary pair Either-or with three statements One of the pair is provable Sometimes neither conclusion follows on its own, but they are exact opposites. Then one of them is true in every picture, and the answer is 'Either I or II follows'. Only two shapes of pairs qualify. Always test each conclusion alone first.

title: Spot the opposite pair
text: Spot the opposite pair Look for (All, Some-not) or (Some, No) on the same two terms. Then test each alone. Syllogism

title.wrong: Choosing either-or when one conclusion follows alone.
title.right: Test each conclusion alone first. If one follows, choose 'Only I' or 'Only II'.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Treating 'No' and 'Some-not' as an opposite pair.
title.right: They can both be false. Only (All, Some-not) and (Some, No) are opposites.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Pairing conclusions that use different terms.
title.right: Both conclusions must use the same two terms.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Treating 'All' and 'No' as a pair.
title.right: Both are false when A only partly overlaps B.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Skipping the pair check because the statements are long.
title.right: Extra statements only matter in the alone test. The pair shape decides the rest.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title: Only-a-few and definite-case rulings — Syllogism
text: Only-a-few and definite-case rulings Only-a-few direct consequences Only-a-few + All chain 'A few / Many' = plain Some Only-a-few with possibility and No statements Two only-a-few statements 'Only a few A are B' means two things at once: some A are B and some A are not B. 'A few' and 'Many' mean plain 'Some'. Split the statement first. Then treat it like any other syllogism.

title: Split on sight
text: Split on sight Rewrite every 'Only a few A are B' as two lines: Some A are B, and Some A are not B. Then solve as normal. Syllogism

title.wrong: Reading 'A few' or 'Many' as 'only a few'.
title.right: They mean plain 'Some'. No outside part is guaranteed.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Assuming 'only a few A are B' says something about B outside A.
title.right: It only fixes the A side. B outside A is undecided.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Passing the outside-A member through 'All B are C'.
title.right: Only the A-and-B member travels. The outside member may or may not be a C.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Thinking 'only a few' allows 'All A are B'.
title.right: It guarantees an A outside B, so 'All A are B' is false.

text: [object Object] Syllogism

title.wrong: Joining two only-a-few statements.
title.right: The overlaps can be different members. Nothing joins.

title: Venn Diagrams
text: Venn Diagrams · Reasoning · Two sets, find the rest · Two sets, find the overlap · Sets in percent · Largest or smallest overlap · Three sets, at least one or none · Exactly two of three · Numbers written in each part · Pick the right diagram

title: What a Venn diagram encodes — Venn Diagrams
text: What a Venn diagram encodes Phrase to set expression Reading region numbers Counting regions Not and at most Neither, nor and exactly one A Venn diagram is a picture of groups. Each circle is one group. Where two circles overlap, the members belong to both groups. First learn to read regions, then learn to add them.

title: Two-set union
text: Two-set union The overlap is counted twice on the right, so subtract it once. |A B| = |A| + |B| - |A B| Venn Diagrams

title: Only A
text: Only A Only A is A minus the overlap. |A B| = |A| - |A B| Venn Diagrams

title: Number of parts
text: Number of parts n circles make 2 to the power n parts, including the outside. 2^n Venn Diagrams

title: Write numbers into the regions
text: Write numbers into the regions Do not keep numbers in your head. Write each one in its region. The answer is then a single sum. Venn Diagrams

title: Shade and compare
text: Shade and compare For a 'which expression' question, shade the phrase first. Then shade each option. Pick the match. Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Adding 35 (tea) and 30 (coffee) and calling it the number who like a drink.
title.right: The overlap is counted twice. Subtract it once: 35 + 30 − 10 = 55.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Reading 'like tea' as 'like only tea'.
title.right: 'Like tea' includes the overlap. 'Only tea' removes it.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Forgetting the outside region.
title.right: People who like neither drink sit outside both circles. Total minus union gives them.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Counting three circles as 7 parts in all.
title.right: There are 7 parts inside the circles and 1 outside, so 8 in all.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Shading A ∪ B when the phrase says 'A and B'.
title.right: 'And' means the overlap only. 'Or' means both circles together.

title: Two-circle counting — Venn Diagrams
text: Two-circle counting Union and neither Find the overlap Percentages in two sets Biggest and smallest overlap Exactly one group Two circles make four parts: only A, only B, both, and neither. Every two-circle question is a sum or a difference of these four parts. Fill them in, then read off the answer.

title: Two-set union
text: Two-set union The overlap is counted twice on the right, so subtract it once. |A B| = |A| + |B| - |A B| Venn Diagrams

title: Only A
text: Only A Only A is A minus the overlap. |A B| = |A| - |A B| Venn Diagrams

title: Neither
text: Neither Everyone outside both circles. = - |A B| Venn Diagrams

title: Exactly one
text: Exactly one Only A plus only B. |A| + |B| - 2|A B| Venn Diagrams

title: Add the four parts to check
text: Add the four parts to check After you fill only A, both, only B and neither, add them. If the sum is not the total, one part is wrong. Venn Diagrams

title: Overlap limits
text: Overlap limits The overlap can never be more than the smaller group. It can never be less than A + B − total. Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Adding 90 + 70 and calling 160 the union.
title.right: The overlap is counted twice. Union = 90 + 70 − 40 = 120.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Treating 'both' as 'only both'.
title.right: 'Both' is the overlap. 'Only A' removes it from A.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Forgetting to subtract the union from the total to get neither.
title.right: Neither = total − union.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Giving a negative number as the smallest overlap.
title.right: If A + B − total is negative, the smallest overlap is 0.

text: [object Object] Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Mixing percent and headcount in one sum.
title.right: Change all numbers to percent, or all to counts, first.

title: Three-circle counting — Venn Diagrams
text: Three-circle counting Union and none Exactly two groups Find one region Find the total of the groups Exactly one group At least two groups Three circles make eight parts: seven inside and one outside. The union formula adds the singles, subtracts the pairs and adds the triple back. Then 'exactly one', 'exactly two' and 'none' are simple sums.

title: Three-set union
text: Three-set union Add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple back. |A B C| = |A| - |A B| + |A B C| Venn Diagrams

title: Exactly two
text: Exactly two Sum of the pair figures minus three times the triple. |A B| - 3|A B C| Venn Diagrams

title: At least two
text: At least two Exactly two plus the triple. |A B| - 2|A B C| Venn Diagrams

title: Exactly one
text: Exactly one Remove the multi-group members from the union. |A B C| - - Venn Diagrams

title: Strip the triple
text: Strip the triple For 'exactly two', take the pair numbers and remove the triple three times. It works because each pair holds the triple once. Venn Diagrams

title: Fill the centre first
text: Fill the centre first Start with the all-three part. Then fill the pairs, then the singles. Each step needs only the numbers you already have. Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Using the pair numbers as 'exactly two'.
title.right: Each pair includes the triple. Exactly two = sum of pairs − 3 × triple.

title.wrong: Forgetting to add the triple back in the union formula.
title.right: Union = singles − pairs + triple. The triple must be added once.

title.wrong: Finding 'only A' as A − AB − AC without the triple.
title.right: The triple is subtracted twice there. Add it back: A − AB − AC + ABC.

title.wrong: Taking the union as the final answer for 'none'.
title.right: None = total − union.

title.wrong: Not checking for a negative part.
title.right: Every part must be 0 or more. A negative part means a slip.

title: Choosing the correct diagram — Venn Diagrams
text: Choosing the correct diagram Nested chain Two subsets in a bigger set Partial overlaps Mixed: inside and crossing Unrelated words Some questions give three words and ask which picture shows them. Judge each pair of words on its own. The pair is nested, overlapping or separate. The correct picture agrees on every pair.

title: One pair at a time
text: One pair at a time Never judge the whole picture at once. Decide each pair, then pick the option that agrees with all three pairs. Venn Diagrams

title: Big class first
text: Big class first Find the widest word first. Draw it as the big circle. Then place the other words inside, across, or outside it. Venn Diagrams

title.wrong: Drawing engineers inside females because you thought of women engineers.
title.right: Male engineers exist too. So engineers cross females, and are not inside.

title.wrong: Making two types, like cats and dogs, overlap.
title.right: No cat is a dog. Draw two separate circles inside the class.

title.wrong: Judging the whole picture at once.
title.right: Check one pair at a time. Drop an option as soon as one pair is wrong.

title.wrong: Nesting words that only sometimes belong together.
title.right: Nest only when every X is a Y. Otherwise draw crossing circles.

title.right: Cats and dogs both sit inside animals. Draw the big circle.
